members.name: normal_pdf_f32
members.summary: The standard normal density exp(-x^2 / 2) / sqrt(2 pi), in float32 arithmetic, branch-free so the loop around it vectorises four lanes wide.
members.extended:
exp(-s) = 2^n * e^r,   s = x^2 / 2,   n = -round(s / ln 2),   |r| <= ln2 / 2

s is carried as two floats: s = h * a rounded (h = a / 2) and, negated,
what that rounding dropped, fma(-h, a, s), exact.  The low part joins the
reduced argument together with the low half of n * ln 2 (Cody-Waite:
n * ln2_hi is exact and s + n * ln2_hi cancels exactly), so r is rounded
once, at its own size.  e^r is 1 + r * P(r), P of degree 5 fitted to 3e-9.

2^n is added straight into the exponent field of e^r.  Adding 1.5 * 2^23
+ 64 rounds -s / ln 2 to an integer and leaves n + 64 in the low bits, so
the scale is a shift and an integer add, and e^r * 2^(n + 64) is a normal
float for every n the clamp allows.  The 2^-64 is folded into the
1 / sqrt(2 pi) of the last multiply, so a density that underflows
(|x| > 13.39) is rounded once, into the subnormals, instead of being
rounded there and then multiplied again.

|x| is clamped to 14.5, past the point where the density rounds to zero
(14.36), which keeps x^2 and n in range for any input: +-inf and NaN give
0, as huge finite inputs do.

members.name: parallel_chunk_count
members.summary: Call `fn(begin, end)` over `[0, n)` in contiguous chunks, in parallel.

parameters.name: grain
parameters.description: Smallest chunk worth handing to another core.  Below two of them the loop runs inline on the caller: dispatching costs a few microseconds, which a small loop never earns back.

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: `void(std::size_t begin, std::size_t end)`.  Must not throw — an exception cannot cross a libdispatch worker — and must write only what its own range owns.

notes:
Chunks are `n * i / chunks` to `n * (i + 1) / chunks`, so they differ
in size by at most one iteration and together cover `[0, n)` exactly.

There are up to four chunks per worker, not one.  Apple silicon mixes
performance and efficiency cores — an M1 Pro is 6 + 2 — and an efficiency
core runs this kind of loop about three times slower.  With one chunk per
core, the wall time was the efficiency cores' share: the exact GELU on
524k elements took 0.40 ms where the performance cores alone finish in
half that.  Smaller chunks let libdispatch hand the fast cores more of
them.  A chunk is never smaller than `grain`.

members.name: parallel_workers
members.summary: Number of chunks a parallel loop may split into on this machine.

returns.description: The logical core count, at least 1.

members.name: permute_copy
members.signature: void permute_copy(const int * in, int * out, const int & in_shape, const int & perm, int elem)
members.summary: Copies a tensor of `elem`-byte elements into a permuted, densely-packed output buffer using the supplied axis permutation.
members.extended:
The output is the input viewed through its C-order strides reordered by
`perm`, packed by `strided::pack` — axes merged, contiguous runs
moved by memcpy, a merged 2-D transpose copied in tiles.  This is an
out-of-place layout transform — there is no in-place fast path.

Permutation moves bytes and never reads a value, so one entry point keyed
by element width serves every dtype.  It used to be one function per
element type, and the backend's switch over them named float16 but not
bfloat16 and had no 8- or 16-byte case for complex, so the backward of a
transpose refused those dtypes on the CPU while Metal ran them.

**Shape**

`out_shape[d] == in_shape[perm[d]]` for every `d`.

parameters.name: in
parameters.description: Source buffer laid out densely (C-order) according to `in_shape`.

parameters.name: out
parameters.description: Destination buffer.  Caller must pre-allocate `numel(in_shape) * elem` bytes.  May not alias `in`.

parameters.name: in_shape
parameters.description: Shape of the source tensor.  An empty vector is treated as a 0-D scalar and produces a single-element copy.

parameters.name: perm
parameters.description: Axis permutation of length `in_shape.size()`.  `perm[d]` names the source axis whose extent becomes output axis `d`.  Must be a valid permutation of `[0, ndim)`.

examples:
``perm = {2, 0, 1}`` over ``in_shape = {H, W, C}`` yields a CHW output.
``perm = {0, 2, 3, 1}`` over ``in_shape = {N, C, H, W}`` performs an NHWC
re-layout.
notes:
Cost is one pass over the bytes plus one odometer step per run, not per
element; a permutation that keeps the last axis in place moves whole rows.
Single-threaded.

members.name: prod_axis_f32
members.signature: void prod_axis_f32(const float * in, float * out, int outer, int reduce_dim, int inner)
members.summary: Reduces a single axis by multiplicative product into a packed `(outer, inner)` output.
members.extended:
Identity element is `1`; an empty reduce dimension yields `1` per cell.
Uses the generic `axis_reduce` template — there is no vDSP equivalent.
Note that floating-point products are not associative, so the result is
deterministic only for a fixed loop order (the kernel iterates `r` from
`0` to `reduce_dim - 1`).

**Math**

$$\text{out}[o, i] = \prod_{r=0}^{\text{reduce\_dim}-1} \text{in}[o, r, i].$$

notes:
Overflow and underflow are unchecked.  Callers that require `log-sum-exp`
style stability must compute the product in log space themselves.

members.name: replace_nonfinite
members.summary: `out[i] = in[i]` with NaN, +inf and -inf replaced, over `n` words.
members.extended:
The replacements arrive already in the format's own bits.  The caller
rounds each double the way a cast to the dtype would (through float for
the 16-bit formats, as the reference framework's half types do), so a
value the format cannot hold becomes its infinity, as the reference
framework's cast makes it.  Every other word is copied bit for bit:
-0, subnormals and NaN payloads are untouched where they are not
replaced.

A complex tensor is passed as its `2 n` interleaved parts.  Each part
is replaced on its own, which is the reference framework's rule for
complex input.

members.name: rms_norm_backward_f32
members.signature: void rms_norm_backward_f32(const float * x, const float * gamma, const float * saved_rstd, const float * g, float * dx, float * dgamma, int outer, int N)
members.summary: Single-precision RMSNorm backward — produces input and weight gradients.
members.extended:
Reuses the saved per-row `rstd` to avoid recomputing the row's RMS.
`dgamma` is *accumulated*; callers reducing over multiple sub-batches
must zero it once at the start.  `dx` is written fully (not accumulated).

**Math**

With $r = \text{rstd}$ and $c = \sum_j \gamma_j g_j x_j$,
$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_i} = r \!\left(\gamma_i g_i - \frac{x_i r^2 c}{N}\right),
  \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \gamma_i} = \sum_{\text{rows}} g_i x_i r.$$

parameters.description: Original forward input of shape `(outer, N)`.

parameters.name: saved_rstd
parameters.description: Per-row reciprocal RMS from the matching forward call.

members.name: rms_norm_forward_f32
members.signature: void rms_norm_forward_f32(const float * x, const float * gamma, float * y, float * saved_rstd, int outer, int N, double eps)
members.summary: Single-precision RMSNorm forward — divides each row by its root-mean-square magnitude and scales by a per-feature gain.
members.extended:
Unlike LayerNorm there is no mean subtraction and no bias parameter, so the
kernel only stores `rstd = 1/sqrt(mean(x^2) + eps)` per row.  This makes
RMSNorm faster and is the form used in many modern transformer variants.

**Math**

$$y_i = \gamma_i \frac{x_i}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_j x_j^2 + \varepsilon}}.$$

**References**

Zhang & Sennrich, "Root Mean Square Layer Normalization" (NeurIPS 2019).

members.name: sgemm
members.signature: void sgemm(bool transA, bool transB, int M, int N, int K, float alpha, const float * A, int lda, const float * B, int ldb, float beta, float * C, int ldc)
members.summary: Single-precision general matrix multiply (GEMM).
members.extended:
Computes $C \leftarrow \alpha (A B) + \beta C$ in row-major layout using
Accelerate's `cblas_sgemm`.  Each transpose flag is mapped to the
corresponding `CBLAS_TRANSPOSE` enum (`CblasNoTrans` / `CblasTrans`)
at zero copy cost — the BLAS kernel selects an alternate inner loop for
transposed operands.

**Math**

$$ C_{ij} \leftarrow \alpha \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} A_{ik} B_{kj} + \beta C_{ij} $$

**References**

BLAS Reference (Netlib), Accelerate.framework `cblas_sgemm`.

parameters.name: transA, transB
parameters.description: Whether $A$ or $B$ should be transposed before the multiply.

parameters.name: M, N, K
parameters.description: Output is $M \times N$; the contracted dimension is $K$, so $A \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times K}$ and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N}$ (before optional transposition).

parameters.name: alpha, beta
parameters.description: Linear-combination coefficients.  Use $\alpha = 1, \beta = 0$ for a pure multiply; nonzero $\beta$ enables fused accumulate-into-C.

parameters.name: C
parameters.description: Row-major output buffer; updated in place when $\beta \neq 0$.

parameters.name: lda, ldb, ldc
parameters.description: Leading dimensions (row stride in elements) of $A$, $B$, $C$.

notes:
Single-threaded on Apple Silicon for small/medium sizes; Accelerate
dispatches to AMX (matrix coprocessor) for large GEMMs automatically.

Computes $y \leftarrow \alpha (A x) + \beta y$ in row-major layout via
Accelerate's `cblas_sgemv`.  Significantly cheaper than `sgemm` for
vector right-hand sides because the inner loop stays in cache.

**Math**

$$ y_i \leftarrow \alpha \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} A_{ij} x_j + \beta y_i $$

**References**

members.name: strsm
members.signature: void strsm(bool upper, bool unit_diag, int M, int N, const float * A, int lda, float * B, int ldb)
members.summary: Single-precision triangular solve with a matrix right-hand side (TRSM).
members.extended:
Overwrites $B$ with $X = A^{-1} B$, where $A$ is an $M \times M$
triangular matrix on the left and $B$ is $M \times N$, both row-major.
Only the triangle named by `upper` is read; `unit_diag` treats the
diagonal as ones without reading it.  Dispatches to Accelerate's
`cblas_strsm` with side Left, no transpose and $\alpha = 1$.

**Math**

For upper $A$, back substitution:
$$ x_i = \Big(b_i - \sum_{j > i} A_{ij} x_j\Big) / A_{ii} $$

**References**

Accelerate.framework `cblas_strsm`.

parameters.name: upper
parameters.description: Whether $A$ is upper (back substitution) or lower (forward substitution) triangular.

parameters.name: unit_diag
parameters.description: Treat the diagonal of $A$ as all ones.

parameters.name: B
parameters.description: Row-major right-hand sides, replaced by the solution.

notes:
No singularity check.  An exactly-zero diagonal entry divides by zero,
so the solution carries the IEEE result ($\pm\infty$, or NaN for
$0 / 0$) — the reference framework's answer for a singular triangle.
LAPACK's `?trtrs` driver checks the diagonal first and reports
`info > 0` without solving; that is the difference that matters here.

members.name: sum_axis_f32
members.signature: void sum_axis_f32(const float * in, float * out, int outer, int reduce_dim, int inner)
members.summary: Reduces a single axis by summation into a packed `(outer, inner)` output.
members.extended:
For each `(o, i)` pair the kernel walks the reduce dimension contiguously
when `inner == 1` and dispatches to Accelerate's `vDSP_sve` for a
vectorised compensated-sum implementation; in the strided case it falls
back to the scalar `axis_reduce` template with identity `0`.

**Math**

$$\text{out}[o, i] = \sum_{r=0}^{\text{reduce\_dim}-1} \text{in}[o, r, i].$$

**See Also**

max_axis_f32, min_axis_f32, prod_axis_f32 : Companion reductions sharing the
    same `(outer, reduce_dim, inner)` layout convention.

parameters.name: in
parameters.description: Source buffer laid out as `(outer, reduce_dim, inner)` in row-major order.

parameters.name: out
parameters.description: Destination buffer of shape `(outer, inner)`; written densely.

parameters.name: outer
parameters.description: Product of all dimensions strictly before the reduce axis.  May be `0`.

parameters.name: reduce_dim
parameters.description: Size of the axis being summed.  A value of `0` yields `0` per cell (the additive identity).

parameters.name: inner
parameters.description: Product of all dimensions strictly after the reduce axis.

notes:
The contiguous fast path uses `vDSP_sve` which performs a vectorised
single-pass summation on Apple Silicon NEON.  Numerical results may differ
from the scalar loop by a few ULP for very long reductions but are typically
stabler.

members.signature: ::mlx::core::array put_along_axis_last_write_wins(const ::mlx::core::array & b, const ::mlx::core::array & i, const ::mlx::core::array & v, int d)
members.summary: `put_along_axis` with last-write-wins tie-breaking along `d`.
members.extended:
When `i` names a destination position along `d` more than once in the
same off-`d` fibre, `mlx::core::put_along_axis` dispatches one GPU
thread per update and lets them race.  Under `set_deterministic(True)`,
scattering the update's coordinate `k in [0, K)` along `d` with
`mlx_scatter_max` selects the highest `k` that targeted each destination
slot — an associative, order-independent integer reduction — and
`take_along_axis` reads `v` at that `k`, matching the CPU's
sequential `0 .. K - 1` overwrite loop.

members.summary: A whole-numbered sample position `v` (already floored or rounded) as an index, whatever `v` is.  NaN reads as 0 and a position past the int64 range saturates at its end — the reference reads its float positions this way, and so lands a NaN coordinate on sample 0.  Casting an infinite or out-of-range float is undefined behaviour, and the CPU grid_sample went on to add 1 to the saturated int: `grid_sample` at x = inf or 1e10 died with SIGBUS (LCD-420).  Callers compare the index with the extent before it addresses anything, and step to a neighbour with `next_index`.

members.summary: The update that leaves a position as it was, which is what an out-of-range update becomes before it is scattered. The index may be shorter than `base` on every axis but `dim` and
shorter than `src` on every axis — the reference's rule, and the CPU's.
MLX's axis scatters want all three to agree off `dim` and raised
"[broadcast_shapes] Shapes (4) and (2) cannot be broadcast" for a valid
call.  So `src` is cut to the index's extent, the scatter runs on the
matching corner of `base`, and the corner is written back.

members.name: scatter_places_nothing
members.summary: MLX's multi-axis scatter (`scatter_add`, `scatter_max` and the rest, one index array per axis) checks each update slice against the base's extents before it counts the updates.  A base with an empty axis therefore raised "[scatter] Updates with shape (0,1,1) are too large for array with shape (0,0)" — the backward of diagonal, interpolate and grid_sample over an empty input, and scatter_reduce into an empty base.  With nothing to place, or nowhere to place it, the scatter is the base.  Every multi-axis scatter on the GPU stream goes through one of these.

members.signature: int bernoulli_op(const int & shape, double p, Dtype dt, Device device, Generator * gen)
members.summary: Allocates a tensor of independent Bernoulli$(p)$ samples.
members.extended:
Each element is independently drawn as `1` with probability $p$
and `0` with probability $1 - p$.

**Math**

$$x_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p), \quad
  \Pr(x_i = 1) = p, \quad \Pr(x_i = 0) = 1 - p$$

**See Also**

`lucid.distributions.Bernoulli` — higher-level
    distribution object built on top of this op.

                                        py::arg("slope") = 0.01);

members.name: bitwise_and_op
members.signature: int bitwise_and_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Element-wise bitwise AND.
members.extended:
Computes `out[i] = a[i] & b[i]` for every element.  Defined on
integer (`I8`/`I16`/`I32`/`I64`) and `Bool` dtypes; on Bool
inputs the result is equivalent to logical AND.

Non-differentiable: bitwise operations have no meaningful gradient on
integer manifolds, so no autograd node is registered.

**Math**

$$
  \mathrm{out}[i] = a[i] \,\wedge_{\text{bit}}\, b[i].
$$

**References**

NumPy `numpy.bitwise_and`.

**See Also**

bitwise_or_op, bitwise_xor_op

parameters.name: a, b
parameters.description: Operands of identical shape, integer-or-Bool dtype, and device.

returns.description: Tensor of the same shape and dtype as the inputs.

raises.description: If shapes/devices differ, or if the input dtype is not integer or Bool.

notes:
* No broadcasting — shapes must match exactly.
* Floating-point inputs are rejected at the dispatch layer.

members.name: bitwise_left_shift_op
members.signature: int bitwise_left_shift_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Element-wise left shift.
members.extended:
Computes `out[i] = a[i] << b[i]` for every element.  Defined only on
signed integer dtypes (`I8`/`I16`/`I32`/`I64`); `Bool` is
rejected because shifting a bit has no defined meaning.

Non-differentiable: no autograd node is registered.

**Math**

$$
  \mathrm{out}[i] = a[i] \cdot 2^{b[i]}.
$$
Out-of-range shift amounts follow the underlying C++ `operator<<`
semantics for signed integers; callers should clamp `b` to
`[0, bitwidth)` to stay portable.

**References**

NumPy `numpy.left_shift`.

**See Also**

bitwise_right_shift_op

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Value to shift.  Signed integer dtype.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Shift amount per element.  Must match `a` in shape, dtype, and device.

returns.description: Tensor of the same shape and dtype as the inputs.

raises.description: If shapes/devices differ, or if the input dtype is not one of `I8`/`I16`/`I32`/`I64`.

notes:
* Floating-point and Bool inputs are rejected at the dispatch layer.
* No broadcasting — shapes must match exactly.

members.name: bitwise_or_op
members.signature: int bitwise_or_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Element-wise bitwise OR.
members.extended:
Computes `out[i] = a[i] | b[i]` for every element.  Defined on
integer and `Bool` dtypes; on Bool inputs this is equivalent to
logical OR.

Non-differentiable: no autograd node is registered.

**Math**

$$
  \mathrm{out}[i] = a[i] \,\vee_{\text{bit}}\, b[i].
$$

**References**

NumPy `numpy.bitwise_or`.

**See Also**

bitwise_and_op, bitwise_xor_op

parameters.name: a, b
parameters.description: Operands of identical shape, integer-or-Bool dtype, and device.

returns.description: Tensor of the same shape and dtype as the inputs.

raises.description: If shapes/devices differ, or if the input dtype is not integer or Bool.

members.name: bitwise_right_shift_op
members.signature: int bitwise_right_shift_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Element-wise right shift.
members.extended:
Computes `out[i] = a[i] >> b[i]` for every element.  Defined only on
signed integer dtypes (`I8`/`I16`/`I32`/`I64`); `Bool` is
rejected.  On signed inputs the shift is arithmetic (sign-extending),
matching the C++ `operator>>` convention used by the backend.

Non-differentiable: no autograd node is registered.

**Math**

$$
  \mathrm{out}[i] = \left\lfloor a[i] / 2^{b[i]} \right\rfloor.
$$
For negative `a[i]` the result is the floor of the true division,
i.e. the standard arithmetic-shift result.

**References**

NumPy `numpy.right_shift`.

**See Also**

bitwise_left_shift_op

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Value to shift.  Signed integer dtype.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Shift amount per element.  Must match `a` in shape, dtype, and device.

returns.description: Tensor of the same shape and dtype as the inputs.

raises.description: If shapes/devices differ, or if the input dtype is not one of `I8`/`I16`/`I32`/`I64`.

notes:
* Floating-point and Bool inputs are rejected at the dispatch layer.
* No broadcasting — shapes must match exactly.

members.signature: int bitwise_xor_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Element-wise bitwise XOR.
members.extended:
Computes `out[i] = a[i] ^ b[i]` for every element.  Defined on
integer and `Bool` dtypes; on Bool inputs this is equivalent to
logical exclusive-or.

Non-differentiable: no autograd node is registered.

**Math**

$$
  \mathrm{out}[i] = a[i] \,\oplus_{\text{bit}}\, b[i].
$$

**References**

NumPy `numpy.bitwise_xor`.

**See Also**

bitwise_and_op, bitwise_or_op

members.name: bmm_op
members.signature: int bmm_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Strict 3-D batched matrix multiply: $C_b = A_b \cdot B_b$.
members.extended:
Composite — rank-checked alias of `matmul_op`.  Rejects inputs of
rank $\ne 3$ and demands matching leading batch dimensions so the error
path is crisp.  Gradient flows through `MatmulBackward`.

**Math**

For every batch index $b \in [0, B)$:
$$
  C_{b, i, j} = \sum_{k} A_{b, i, k} \, B_{b, k, j}
$$

**See Also**

`mm_op`, `matmul_op`.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Left operand of shape `(B, M, K)`.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Right operand of shape `(B, K, N)`.  Leading batch `B` must match `a`.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `(B, M, N)`.

raises.description: If either input is null, not exactly 3-D, or batch dimensions disagree.

members.name: broadcast_back_for_reduce
members.signature: int broadcast_back_for_reduce(const int & grad, const int & grad_shape, const int & input_shape, const int & axes, bool keepdims, Dtype dt, Device device)
members.summary: Broadcast `grad` back to `input_shape` after a forward reduction.
members.extended:
The backward pass for any reduction op (`sum`, `mean`, `var`,
...) receives a gradient at the reduced shape and must re-expand it
across the squeezed axes so that the result matches the original input
shape.  This helper performs that expansion, taking the same
`axes` / `keepdims` parameters as the forward call to know which
dimensions to broadcast back along.

**See Also**

`reduce_output_shape` — the inverse direction.

parameters.name: grad
parameters.description: Incoming gradient at the reduced shape.

parameters.name: grad_shape
parameters.description: Shape of `grad`; must equal `reduce_output_shape(input_shape, axes, keepdims)`.

parameters.name: input_shape
parameters.description: Shape to broadcast back to (the original forward input shape).

parameters.name: axes
parameters.description: Axis list used in the forward reduction.

parameters.name: keepdims
parameters.description: Same value as passed to the forward reduction.

returns.description: New storage of shape `input_shape` carrying the expanded gradient.

raises.description: `grad_shape` does not equal the expected reduced shape.

members.summary: Write the broadcast of `src` (shaped as the plan's source) into `dst`.

members.name: broadcast_to_op
members.signature: int broadcast_to_op(const int & a, const int & shape)
members.summary: Broadcast a tensor to a larger shape following NumPy rules.
members.extended:
The input shape is right-aligned with `shape`; size-1 dimensions are
replicated and newly prepended axes are inserted.  If `a` is not
contiguous a copy is made before the broadcast operation runs.

**See Also**

`expand_op` (alias), `BroadcastBackward`.

parameters.name: shape
parameters.description: Target shape.  Must be NumPy-broadcast-compatible with `a.shape`.

returns.description: A tensor of shape `shape` whose values are replicated from `a`.

raises.description: If `a.shape` cannot be broadcast to `shape` (any mismatching axis where neither side is 1).

examples:
``broadcast_to_op([1, 2, 3], (4, 3))`` produces a 4x3 tensor where every
row equals ``[1, 2, 3]``.

members.name: broyden_probe_op
members.signature: BroydenProbeResult broyden_probe_op(const int & residual, const int & step, const int & state, const int & info)
members.summary: Answer all of a Broyden iteration's questions in one pass.
members.extended:
An implicit method solves its stage equations by quasi-Newton iteration,
and each iteration has to decide several things on the host: whether the
residual is small enough to stop, whether the step has fallen below what
the state's precision can represent, whether the linear solve succeeded,
and whether the step is long enough for the rank-one update to be defined.

Written separately, those are four reductions, four temporaries, and -- on
the GPU -- four pipeline flushes.  MLX evaluates lazily, so reading any one
scalar waits for everything queued behind it; measured on an M4 Max, that
wait is around 120 microseconds while the arithmetic it interrupts is
closer to 10.  The flushes, not the arithmetic, are what an implicit solve
spends its time on.  Fusing them costs one flush and no temporaries, and on
the CPU it also drops the intermediate tensors the Python spelling would
allocate.

**See Also**

rk_error_norm_op : the same trade for adaptive step-size control.

parameters.name: residual
parameters.description: Current residual vector.  Defines dtype and device; must be F32 or F64.

parameters.name: step
parameters.description: Proposed Newton step.  Same dtype and device as `residual` and the same element count, though not necessarily the same shape -- the linear solve returns a column, the residual is flat.

parameters.name: state
parameters.description: Current iterate.  Same dtype, device, and element count as `residual`.

parameters.name: info
parameters.description: Status scalar from the linear solve.  Any dtype; read as a number. May be null, for the seeding call made before any solve has happened; `info` then reports zero and only the norms are computed.

returns.description: The scalars, already on the host.

raises.description: If `residual` is neither F32 nor F64.
If `step` or `state` disagrees with `residual` on dtype, device, or element count.

members.name: bucketize_op
members.signature: int bucketize_op(const int & values, const int & boundaries, bool right)
members.summary: Bucket-index lookup: alias of `searchsorted_op` with the operand order flipped to match the bucket-first convention.
members.extended:
Composite — delegates directly to `searchsorted_op(boundaries,
values, right)`.  Not differentiable.

**Math**

$$
  y_{\ldots, j} = \sum_{i} \mathbb{1}\!\left[ b_i \prec v_{\ldots, j} \right]
$$
with $b$ = `boundaries` and the comparison $\prec$ selected by
`right` per `searchsorted_op`.

**See Also**

`searchsorted_op`.

parameters.name: right
parameters.description: If `true`, queries equal to a boundary land in the higher bucket.

returns.description: `int64` tensor of the same shape as `values` whose entries are bucket indices in $[0, \mathrm{len}(\mathrm{boundaries})]$.

members.name: buffer_is_elements
members.summary: Whether `t`'s own buffer, from its first byte, is its elements in row-major order: a contiguous CPU tensor at offset 0 (a run at the start of a larger buffer included), or a Metal tensor that reads all of its family's root.

members.name: cartesian_prod_op
members.summary: Enumerate every combination across a list of 1-D tensors.
members.extended:
Composite over `meshgrid_op` (with `ij` indexing) +
`reshape_op` + `stack_op`.  Builds the n-D grid, flattens
each component, and stacks the flattened columns along a new trailing
axis to produce a `(N, D)` matrix whose rows enumerate the full
Cartesian product in row-major (ij) order.  Gradient flows through
`MeshgridBackward`, `ReshapeBackward`, and `StackBackward`.

**Math**

For input tensors $t^{(0)}, \ldots, t^{(D-1)}$ of lengths
$n_0, \ldots, n_{D-1}$, the output rows are
$$
  \left( t^{(0)}_{i_0}, t^{(1)}_{i_1}, \ldots, t^{(D-1)}_{i_{D-1}} \right),
  \qquad (i_0, \ldots, i_{D-1}) \in \prod_d [0, n_d)
$$
in row-major (lex) order with $i_0$ varying slowest.

**See Also**

`meshgrid_op`, `stack_op`.

parameters.name: tensors
parameters.description: Non-empty list of 1-D tensors.  Lengths may differ.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `(N, D)` where `N = prod(lengths)` and `D` is the number of inputs.  Dtype matches the inputs (must agree).

raises.description: If the input list is empty, any element is null, or any element is not 1-D.

notes:
When determinism is not globally enabled, this function is a no-op
and adds only a single relaxed atomic load to the call site.

members.name: check_version_match
members.signature: void check_version_match(const int & live, int saved_version, int op_name, int input_idx)
members.summary: Verify that a saved tensor's version counter has not advanced.
members.extended:
Compares the current `version()` of the tensor referenced by `live`
against `saved_version`.  When they differ the saved data has been
mutated in place since it was stashed for backward, which would silently
corrupt the gradient — so a `VersionMismatch` is raised naming
the op and input that owns the broken contract.

parameters.name: live
parameters.description: Weak reference to the still-live tensor.  When the referent has been destroyed the check is skipped (no harm if it cannot be mutated after the fact).

parameters.name: saved_version
parameters.description: Version counter value captured when the tensor was saved.

parameters.name: op_name
parameters.description: Name of the op for diagnostic messages (e.g. `"matmul"`).

parameters.name: input_idx
parameters.description: Zero-based index of the offending input within `op_name`.

raises.description: The live counter differs from `saved_version` and the safety override (`is_mutation_on_saved_allowed`) is false.

members.name: cholesky_op
members.signature: int cholesky_op(const int & a, bool upper)
members.summary: Compute the Cholesky factor of a symmetric positive-definite matrix.
members.extended:
Returns the lower-triangular $L$ (default) or upper-triangular $U$ such
that $A = LL^\top$ or $A = U^\top U$ respectively.  Forward dispatches to
LAPACK `*potrf` (CPU) or `mlx::core::linalg::cholesky` (GPU).  Batched
inputs are supported: every dimension except the trailing two is treated
as a batch axis and the factorisation is run independently on each
$N \times N$ slice.

**Math**

$$
  A = LL^\top \quad\text{or}\quad A = U^\top U.
$$
The corresponding reverse-mode rule (Murray 2016) is
$$
  \frac{\partial L}{\partial A} = \tfrac{1}{2}\, L^{-\top}
    \Phi\!\bigl(L^\top \tfrac{\partial L}{\partial L}\bigr) L^{-1},
$$
where $\Phi(M) = \mathrm{tril}(M) + \mathrm{tril}(M, -1)^\top$ copies the
strict lower triangle into the strict upper.  This formula is realised in
the Python wrapper via two triangular solves, not in this engine op.

**Shape**

- `a`: `(..., N, N)`.
- return: `(..., N, N)`.

**See Also**

- `solve_triangular_op` — triangular back/forward substitution used in
  the Python-side Cholesky backward.
- `ldl_factor_op` — analogous factorisation for symmetric indefinite
  matrices.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Square symmetric positive-definite matrix of shape `(..., N, N)`, dtype `F32` or `F64`.

parameters.name: upper
parameters.description: If `true` return the upper factor $U$; otherwise (default) return the lower factor $L$.

returns.description: Triangular Cholesky factor with the same shape and dtype as `a`. The opposite triangle is filled with zeros.

raises.description: If `a` is not at least 2-D, not square, or has a non-float dtype.
If LAPACK `info > 0` — a non-positive pivot was encountered, i.e. `a` is not positive definite (within working precision).

notes:
No autograd node is wired; the returned `TensorImpl` has
`requires_grad = false`.  Gradient-aware Cholesky is provided one layer
up by `lucid.linalg.cholesky`.

members.name: clear_saved
members.summary: CRTP base supplying boilerplate fields and methods to concrete backward nodes with a fixed number of forward inputs.
members.extended:
Inherit as `class FooBackward : public AutogradNode<FooBackward, N>` —
or, more commonly, through the `FuncOp` alias — to obtain
`N`-slot saved-input storage, automatic version validation, and an
engine-friendly `release_saved` implementation.  The derived class
must expose a `static constexpr OpSchema schema_v1` whose `.name`
field identifies the op in error messages and traces, and must
implement `apply` returning one `Storage` per forward
input.

Template Parameters
-------------------
Derived : class
    The concrete backward node class (CRTP self-type).  Must expose a
    `static constexpr` member `schema_v1` with at least a `.name`
    `std::string_view` field.
N_IN : std::size_t
    Number of input tensors the corresponding forward op consumes.
    Determines the compile-time size of `saved_inputs_`,
    `input_shapes_`, `input_tensors_`, and
    `saved_impl_inputs_`.

**See Also**

`Node` — the abstract base whose virtuals this class overrides.
`FuncOp` — alias used by most concrete backward classes.
notes:
**Lifecycle.** The forward op builder constructs an instance, fills
`input_tensors_`, `input_shapes_`, `saved_inputs_`,
`saved_output_`, `dtype_`, and `device_`, then calls
`Node::set_next_edges` and `Node::set_saved_versions`
before attaching the node to the output `TensorImpl` via
`set_grad_fn`.  During backward the engine calls
`validate_versions` then `apply`.  After `apply`
returns, the engine calls `release_saved`, which resets every
`Storage` slot to a default-constructed (zero-byte)
`CpuStorage` so referenced memory can be freed immediately.

**Thread safety.** None.  All access happens on the single backward
thread.

**Slot ordering.** `saved_inputs_` and the gradients returned
from `apply` are ordered to match the forward op's positional
argument list — changing that order is a wire-format break.

attributes.name: kNumInputs
attributes.description: Compile-time constant mirror of `N_IN` for callers that need it as a value (e.g. when constructing the `next_edges` vector).

attributes.name: input_tensors_
attributes.description: Weak references to the original input `TensorImpl` objects, used by `validate_versions` for the inputs saved by value. Weak so the backward graph never extends an input's lifetime.

attributes.name: input_shapes_
attributes.description: Shapes of the forward inputs, captured so that broadcasts and reductions can be inverted in `apply` without needing the live `TensorImpl`.

attributes.name: out_shape_
attributes.description: Shape of the forward output; used to allocate or validate the incoming gradient in `apply`.

attributes.name: dtype_
attributes.description: Dtype of the forward computation.  Gradient tensors are created with this dtype.  Defaults to `Dtype::F32`.

attributes.name: device_
attributes.description: Device of the forward computation.  Gradient tensors live on the same device.  Defaults to `Device::CPU`.

attributes.name: grad_dtypes_
attributes.description: The dtype input `i` had before the forward cast it to `dtype_` for an AMP policy; empty when it was used as given. The cast is part of the op, so the op hands that input's gradient back in this dtype — a view or permute between the input and this node reads it at its own width.  Set only for inputs that take a gradient.

attributes.name: saved_inputs_
attributes.description: Copies of forward input `Storage` values that `apply` reads — for example, the input activations of an element-wise multiply.  Populated by the forward op builder.  The one place a node keeps an input's values: a slot holding them is what `validate_versions` guards and `restore_saved_for_graph` rebuilds from, so a node never keeps an input's values in a member of its own (`tools/check_saved_versions.py`).

attributes.name: saved_output_
attributes.description: Copy of the forward output `Storage`, populated only when the backward formula needs the output activation (sigmoid, softmax, tanh, etc.).  Left as an empty `CpuStorage` when unused.

attributes.name: saved_impl_inputs_
attributes.description: Strong references to the source `TensorImpl` objects. Set in lockstep with `saved_inputs_` so that `Node::apply_for_graph` can call into `grad_fn`-bearing ops when `create_graph=True`.

attributes.name: saved_impl_output_
attributes.description: **Weak** reference to the forward output `TensorImpl`, set only for ops whose graph-mode backward needs the output value (e.g. `SigmoidBackward`).  Deliberately weak: a strong ref here would form a `Node -> output -> grad_fn -> same Node` cycle (the output already owns this node via `grad_fn`), and since the cycle is broken only by `backward()` clearing `grad_fn`, an inference / forward-only loop that never calls backward would retain every per-call graph and eventually OOM.  Holding it weakly keeps the autograd reference graph a pure backward-pointing DAG, so dropping the output cascades the whole graph free.  `create_graph` backward does not read the live output through it any more: a write after forward could have changed it with nothing to show, so `restore_saved_for_graph` drops the handle and the reader rebuilds the output from `saved_output_` with this node as its grad_fn — the case it already covered for an output that was gone.

members.name: clip_inplace_op
members.signature: int clip_inplace_op(const int & a, double lo, double hi)
members.summary: In-place clip / clamp: writes $\mathrm{clip}(x, \mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi})$ back into `a`.
members.extended:
**Math**

$$a_i \leftarrow \min(\mathit{hi}, \max(\mathit{lo}, a_i))$$

**See Also**

`clip_op` — out-of-place counterpart.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Tensor to clip in place.  Must be non-null.

parameters.name: lo
parameters.description: Lower bound; values below `lo` are set to `lo`.

parameters.name: hi
parameters.description: Upper bound; values above `hi` are set to `hi`.

returns.description: The same pointer as `a`.

notes:
Implemented directly (without going through the generic
`inplace_unary` helper) because the two scalar parameters
`lo` / `hi` cannot be threaded through the zero-argument
function-pointer template the other entry points use.

members.name: clip_op
members.signature: int clip_op(const int & a, double min_v, double max_v)
members.summary: Element-wise clamp — returns `a` clipped to the range `[min_v, max_v]` with a fully wired autograd node.
members.extended:
**Math**

$$y_i = \max\bigl(\text{min\_v},\ \min(\text{max\_v},\ x_i)\bigr)$$

**Shape**

Output shape equals input shape (elementwise).

**See Also**

`ClipBackward`.

returns.description: Clamped output tensor with the same shape, dtype, and device as `a`.  Gradient is `g` where `min_v < a < max_v` and zero where `a` saturates either bound.

notes:
Equivalent to reference framework's `clamp` (Lucid uses the name
`clip` for the canonical op).  Saturated positions act as gradient
stoppers — useful for hard-tanh-style activations.

members.name: clone_state_storage
members.signature: int clone_state_storage(const int & src, const int & shape, Dtype dtype, Device device)
members.summary: Deep-copy an optimizer state buffer into a new owning TensorImpl.
members.extended:
Snapshots a state `Storage` (CPU or GPU) into a freshly allocated
`TensorImpl` whose backing buffer is independent of the original.
This is the primitive used by derived optimizers when implementing
`state_buffers()` so that the returned tensors survive any future
in-place updates by `step()`.

**See Also**

overwrite_state_storage : in-place inverse used by
    `load_state_buffers`.

parameters.name: src
parameters.description: Source state buffer.  Must be either `CpuStorage` or `GpuStorage`.  For `GpuStorage` the underlying MLX array is materialised via `eval()` before copying.

parameters.name: shape
parameters.description: Logical shape to attach to the returned `TensorImpl`.  Must match the element count implied by `src`.

parameters.name: dtype
parameters.description: Dtype tag to record on the new `TensorImpl`.

parameters.name: device
parameters.description: Device tag to record on the new `TensorImpl`.

returns.description: A non-leaf tensor whose storage is a deep copy of `src`.

raises.description: If `src` is neither a `CpuStorage` nor a `GpuStorage`.

notes:
CPU copies use `allocate_aligned_bytes` followed by `memcpy`;
GPU copies build an independent MLX array.  In both cases the
resulting buffer can be mutated freely without affecting the source
optimizer state.

members.signature: int clone_storage(const int & s, int numel, Dtype dt, Device device)
members.summary: Allocate a fresh copy of `s` (deep clone).

members.summary: Cast helper: `void*` ↔ `MPSGraphTensor*`.  Each VJP body would otherwise litter every line with `(__bridge MPSGraphTensor*)`.

members.name: attention_workaround_state
members.summary: Attention fused-pass workaround — process-global capability state.
members.extended:
MPSGraph (on some GPU/OS combinations — observed on M1 Pro / macOS 26,
NOT on M4 Max / macOS 27) pattern-matches `softmax(QKᵀ) @ V` onto a
fused-attention kernel that silently miscompiles for a window of shapes.
The emitters dodge it by emitting the value-matmul transposed, but that
costs ~+70% on the attention path — pure waste on unaffected hardware.

A one-time Python probe (`lucid.compile._core.attention_probe`) compiles
a known-bad envelope against an eager reference and sets this state, so the
(expensive) transpose only fires where the defect actually exists:
  -1 = unprobed → default to applying the transpose (always-correct);
   0 = this GPU is unaffected → skip the transpose (fast path);
   1 = this GPU is affected → apply the transpose (correct).
`apply_attention_workaround()` is the predicate the emitters call.

members.name: axes_for_unreduce
members.signature: int axes_for_unreduce(const int & broadcast, const int & target)
members.summary: Compute the axes that need to be reduce-summed in order to go from `broadcast` shape to `target` shape.  Mirrors the eager `broadcast_back_for_reduce`'s axis computation.  Broadcast rules: align right, treat missing leading dims as 1, dims that are 1 in `target` but > 1 in `broadcast` were broadcast.

members.signature: bool bool_attr(const OpNode & node, const char * key, bool def)

members.name: canonicalize_executable
members.signature: int canonicalize_executable(const CompiledExecutable * exe, const TraceIdMap & id_map)
members.summary: Return a copy of `exe` whose `input_ids` and `output_ids` have been translated from the trace's raw `TensorId` space into canonical indices via `id_map.to_canonical`.  Returns an empty pointer if `exe` is null or any id is absent from `id_map`.

members.name: cast_if_needed
members.signature: int * cast_if_needed(int * g, int * t, int target)
members.summary: Cast `t` to `target` if its dtype doesn't already match — no-op otherwise.  Returns the (possibly-cast) tensor.  Used by VJPs to reconcile mixed-dtype operands under autocast: every VJP convention is that all intermediate arithmetic runs in `grad.dataType` (the chain's dominant dtype).  Forward activations like `x` / `gamma` / `beta` cast to that dtype at the VJP prologue; the astype VJP at the param boundary handles the final cast back to the param's master dtype on the way to the optimizer.
members.extended:
Without this reconciliation, under `with autocast(F16)` the
downstream binary builders fail MPSGraph's same-dtype check
(`'mps.multiply' op requires the same element type for all
operands and results`), exposing every VJP that calls
`multiplicationWithPrimaryTensor:` / `additionWithPrimaryTensor:`
/ etc. on a mix of grad (F16) + forward activation (F32 master).

The convention is grad-dominant (not output-dominant) because the
grad's dtype determines the downstream chain's dtype — we minimize
per-VJP casts by aligning to the side that's already in the right
precision for whatever comes next in the backward walk.

members.signature: int * cast_mps_tensor(int * g, int * x, int dst, int * name)

members.signature: int * commit_half_before_widen(int * g, int * x, int dst)
members.summary: Materialise a float16 / bfloat16 tensor's 16-bit representation before widening it to float32.  MPSGraph's MLIR optimizer otherwise folds `cast(op_f16(...), f32)` into `op_f32(...)`, eliding the IEEE binary16 / bfloat16 rounding and finite-range clamp (65504 for float16).

members.name: compile_fused_training_step
members.signature: CompiledExecutable * compile_fused_training_step(const TraceGraph & graph, const int & external_feeds, TensorId loss_id, const int & param_ids, const OptimizerSpec & opt_spec, const int)
members.summary: Compile a single MPSGraph executable that runs the full training step in one dispatch:
members.extended:
loss = loss_fn(model(x), target)
  grad_param[i] = ∂loss / ∂param[i]   ← derived by MPSGraph
  new_param[i], new_state[i, k] = opt_update(param[i], grad_param[i],
                                             state[i, k], ...)

Output layout (in this order):
  1. loss            ← single scalar/tensor produced by the forward.
  2. new_param[i]    ← one per `param_ids[i]`.
  3. new_state[i, k] ← per (param, state-slot-index) — exactly the
                       `state_buf_ids_per_param` layout flattened
                       row-major (i, k).

At run time the caller uses `run_executable_inplace` with the
output_targets = [loss_scratch, params (in order), state_bufs
(flattened)] so the new values overwrite the existing storage.  The
loss is allocated fresh and returned to Python for logging.

parameters.name: graph
parameters.description: Forward trace (model + loss).  Same shape as `compile_trace_with_backward`.

parameters.name: external_feeds
parameters.description: id → impl map for every external feed in `graph`.  Must include every parameter id, every state buffer id, and every per-step scalar id.

parameters.name: loss_id, param_ids :
parameters.description: Forward-graph ids for the scalar loss and the parameters with respect to which the gradient is taken.

parameters.name: state_buf_ids_per_param :
parameters.description: For each param i, the trace ids of its state buffers (in the order each optimizer expects: SGD = [momentum] or empty, Adam = [m, v]).  All must already be in `external_feeds`.

parameters.name: scalar_input_ids :
parameters.description: Per-step scalar feed ids in the order each optimizer expects (Adam / AdamW: [bias1, bias2]; SGD: empty).  These are read at run time as 0-D float feeds.

returns.description: Owns the compiled executable.  `output_ids` = `{loss_id}`; `grad_output_ids` carries one id per (new_param, new_state) output in the order described above.  Returns nullptr on abort.

members.name: compile_generic_fused_step
members.signature: CompiledExecutable * compile_generic_fused_step(const TraceGraph & graph, const int & external_feeds, TensorId loss_id, const int & param_ids, const int & ghost_grad_ids, const int & output_target_ids, int * error_msg)
members.summary: Like `compile_fused_training_step` but the optimizer update math is captured in the same `TraceGraph` as the forward pass — no per-optimizer C++ emit branch.  Each `ghost_grad_id` is a tensor placeholder that the Python wrapper reserved as the "grad input" of the optimizer update; this function binds those placeholders to MPSGraph-derived gradient tensors after the forward has been emitted, then continues emitting the remaining (optimizer) ops which now resolve their grad reads correctly.
members.extended:
Why this exists
---------------
The hardcoded path supports SGD / Adam / AdamW.  Adding RMSprop /
Adagrad / Adadelta / Adamax / NAdam (and any future optimizer) via
the hardcoded path would duplicate the math already expressed by
each `compile_optimizer` subclass.  This function lets the
Python wrapper reuse that math directly — trace it once into the
same graph, then bind the ghost grads here.

Output layout (in order):
  1. loss
  2. one entry per `output_target_ids[i]` (the trace ids of the
     new_param / new_state tensors the optimizer wrote into).

At run time, callers use `run_executable_inplace` with
output_targets = [loss_scratch, param_0, param_1, ...,
state_buf_0_0, state_buf_0_1, ...].

members.name: compile_generic_fused_step_with_vars
members.signature: CompiledExecutable * compile_generic_fused_step_with_vars(const TraceGraph & graph, const int & external_feeds, TensorId loss_id, const int & param_ids, const int & ghost_grad_ids, const int & output_target_ids, const int)
members.summary: ── Stateful-variables variant of compile_generic_fused_step ────────
members.extended:
Same lifecycle and contract as `compile_generic_fused_step` —
the trace covers forward + loss + (ghost-grad → opt update) — but a
designated subset of the *external feeds* is promoted to MPSGraph
**stateful variables** instead of placeholders, and the matching
subset of the trace's *output targets* is bound to `assignVariable`
operations instead of executable graph outputs.

Per-step semantics (when paired with `run_executable_inplace`):

* The transient feeds (model input `x`, loss target, per-step
    scalars) remain regular placeholders — same I/O as before.
  * Each variable feed initialises its variable from the current
    `MTLBuffer` contents of the matching Lucid Tensor at
    *compile* time.  Later steps reuse the variable's persistent
    internal storage; the executable's input list excludes them
    entirely.
  * Each variable write target is emitted as an `assignVariable`
    op (added to `targetOperations`).  Immediately after the
    assignment, a `readVariable` op is included as a regular
    `targetTensor` so the new value can be flushed back to the
    Lucid Tensor's MTLBuffer on each call — keeping
    `model.fc1.weight`-style reads up to date between steps.

Why this wins
-------------
The original `run_executable_inplace` path allocates one fresh
`MTLBuffer` per output target (`newBufferWithLength:`,
~5-30μs × N), wraps it as `MPSGraphTensorData`, runs the
executable, then swaps the Lucid Tensor's MLX array onto the
fresh buffer.  Variables eliminate the per-step buffer
allocation: the readback writes directly into the existing Lucid
Tensor buffer, and the assignment writes happen *inside* the
variable's persistent storage with no host-visible buffer at all.

parameters.name: graph, external_feeds, loss_id, param_ids, ghost_grad_ids, output_target_ids
variable_pairs
parameters.description: Each pair is `(feed_id, write_id)`.  `feed_id` must be in `external_feeds`; `write_id` must appear in `output_target_ids` (or be the trace output bound to a compile-time-known write slot for this variable).  The feed's initial values are snapshot from the Lucid Tensor's current MTLBuffer at compile time.  Empty vector → equivalent to `compile_generic_fused_step`.

returns.description: Owns the compiled executable.  `input_ids` excludes every `feed_id` in `variable_pairs`; `grad_output_ids` excludes every `write_id` and replaces them with the corresponding `readVariable` outputs (so `run_executable_inplace` can still bind the Lucid Tensor buffers as targets). `nullptr` on abort.

members.summary: Unary VJP skeleton — for ops with exactly one differentiable input.
members.extended:
`body` is invoked as `body(graph, x_t, grad_t)` and must return
the gradient w.r.t. `x`, OR `nil` to abort the VJP.  On success
the helper calls `BackwardContext::accumulate_grad(x_id, dx)`
and returns `true`; on any guard failure it returns `false`.

Mixed-dtype reconciliation under autocast (the chain-dominant
convention — see `cast_if_needed`): by default the forward
activation `x_t` is cast to `grad_t.dataType` before the body
runs, so all body arithmetic is in one dtype.  VJPs that genuinely
need the original forward dtype (e.g. `AstypeVjp` which casts the
grad *back* to the input dtype) opt out by passing
`cast_forward_to_grad=false`.

Returns `0` when `exe` is `nullptr`.  Useful for binding-layer
validation before invoking `run_executable`.

members.signature: int * graph_fill_out_of_range(int * g, int * gathered, int * in_range)

members.signature: int * graph_first_extreme(int * g, int * x, int axis, bool is_max)
members.summary: The first position of the largest (`is_max`) or smallest value along `axis` (kept, length one).  MPSGraph's arg reductions start from the type's extreme and keep the first value that passes it, so a slice that is all -inf (argmax), all +inf (argmin), or all the integer type's lowest / highest value named -1 (LCD-461).  Every value of such a slice is equal, and the first position, 0, is the answer.

members.signature: int * graph_gather_along_axis(int * g, int axis, int * data, int * idx, int * name)

members.signature: int * graph_gather_sorted(int * g, int * x, int * order, int axis)
members.summary: `x` read at `order` along `axis` — a sort's values, every bit of them: MPSGraph's own gather rounded int64 through float32, so 2^40 + 3 came back as 2^40 (LCD-435, `_DataMovement.h`).

members.summary: Whether MPSGraph's `op` family moves every value of `dt` unchanged.

members.name: graph_order_key
members.summary: An int32 key that orders `x` as eager orders it — ±0 equal, -inf the lowest value, every NaN equal and above +inf — and never takes INT32_MIN, so a selection can retire a position by writing INT32_MIN there without meeting a real value.  nil for a dtype with no such key: int32 and wider integers fill every int32 value, and bool is not ordered by `topk`.
members.extended:
A float is keyed by its bits.  A non-negative float's bits already order
as int32; a negative float's grow with its magnitude, so their low 31 bits
are flipped.  -inf keys to INT32_MIN + 2^23 - 1, the lowest key, and only
a NaN's bits could reach INT32_MIN.

members.name: graph_pixel
members.signature: GraphPixel graph_pixel(int * g, int * px, int * py, long long H, long long W, bool zero_padding)
members.summary: The pixel at `(px, py)`, clamped onto the image for the read.  A NaN coordinate is taken as 0 first: casting NaN to an integer is undefined and comparing it is false everywhere, so it otherwise read an unknown pixel. Eager casts after rounding, and Apple silicon's float-to-int conversion turns NaN into 0 on both devices, so eager reads position 0 there and counts it inside — a NaN nearest sample is that pixel, a NaN bilinear sample NaN through its weights.  `inside` is computed only for zero padding, the one mode whose outside reads are replaced.

members.signature: int * graph_scatter_identity(int * g, GraphScatter op, int dt)
members.summary: The update that leaves a held value as it was, which is what an out-of-range update becomes before it is scattered at the safe index. For a sum that is -0.0, not +0.0: `x + -0.0` is `x` for every `x`, -0.0 included.  nil when the dtype has no such value here (complex).

No in-range position can take a write and keep its value, so an out-of-range write is aimed at a one-wide sink slab appended past the end of `axis` and cut off again — eager's `gpu_sink_index` / `with_sink_slab`.  nil when MPSGraph cannot write the dtype exactly.

Half precision is widened to float32 first — exact, so the order is the same — because MPSGraph's compare-to-zero pass rejects a float16 `equal` with a warning on every compile ("ConvertBinaryCompareToZero expects the second operand to be zero").

members.signature: CacheKey make_cache_key(const TraceGraph & graph, const int)
members.summary: Build a `CacheKey` from a `TraceGraph`.
members.extended:
Walks `graph.ops` once, copying the name + first-output meta from
each node.  Device is taken from the most recent non-empty output;
it is the caller's responsibility to ensure the trace is
single-device (the MpsBuilder rejects mixed-device traces before
hashing).

fills `CacheKey::feeds`.
`explicit_outputs` are the trace ids the caller will read back, in
order; they fill `CacheKey::outputs`.
When `id_map` is non-null, it is populated with the raw-to-canonical
and canonical-to-raw `TensorId` bijection for this trace.

members.signature: bool matches_recorded_shape(int * t, const OpNode & node)
members.summary: True when `t`'s static shape is the shape the trace recorded for the node's first output.  An emitter whose op is lowered with options MPSGraph may size differently (ceil-mode pooling) declines rather than hand the next op a tensor of another shape.

members.name: materialize_matmul_splat
members.signature: int * materialize_matmul_splat(int * g, int * t, bool is_splat)
members.summary: Materialize a compile-time constant splat before feeding it to `matrixMultiplicationWithPrimaryTensor`.  When a splat constant is shared between an elementwise op and a matmul, MPSGraph passes a stride-0 broadcast MPSNDArray into `MPSNDArrayMatrixMultiplication`, which asserts at `MPSNDArrayMatrixMultiplication.mm:7162` ("A and B index not found.").  `bandPart(-1, -1)` keeps every diagonal while forcing MPSGraph to materialize the 2-D matrix axes.

A binding that hands Python a tensor's values (`item` / `tolist` / `numpy` / bytes / a DLPack capsule) calls `note_host_read` first; one that makes a new tensor from an existing one returns it through `traced_derive`.  The source scan in `lucid/test/unit/compile/test_trace_entry_points.py` holds every TensorImpl binding to this.

Used by the walker to seed `∂loss/∂loss = 1` before iterating the

w/ `reduction='none'`) seeds correctly; using
`constantWithScalar:dataType:` (0-D) would broadcast on the first

members.signature: int * pad_or_identity(int * g, int * x, int * left, int * right, int mode, double value, int * name)

members.name: promote_to_float_output
members.signature: int * promote_to_float_output(int * g, int * x, const OpNode & node)
members.summary: Eager promotes the integer or bool operand of a floating op — `exp` of an int32 tensor is float32 — and the trace records that promoted output dtype, but the operand reaches the emitter un-promoted.  Without the cast the graph ran `exp` on integers and wrote the result into a float32 buffer: `exp(int32)` was off by 403, `mean(int64)` by 0.83.  Only a floating output over a non-floating input is touched, so `abs(int)` and `sum(int)` keep their integer arithmetic.

members.name: propagate_zero_splat
members.signature: void propagate_zero_splat(BuilderContext & ctx, const OpNode & node)
members.summary: Carry a ±0 / ±1 splat mark from `node`'s input to its output.  `emit_node` calls it after every op, so the rule lives in one place.

members.summary: `feeds` with every noted draw replaced by a fresh one, drawn in the order the trace drew them.  Returns `feeds` itself when none is.

members.name: relabel_executable
members.signature: CompiledExecutable * relabel_executable(const CompiledExecutable * exe, int input_ids, int output_ids)
members.summary: Return a shallow copy of `exe` sharing the underlying `MPSGraphExecutable*` (and any retained `source_graph`) and all shape/dtype/slot metadata, with `input_ids` and `output_ids` replaced by the given vectors.  Returns `nullptr` when `exe` is `nullptr` or when the replacement vector lengths do not match the existing `input_ids` / `output_ids` lengths.

members.name: reshape_dynamic_aware
members.signature: int * reshape_dynamic_aware(int * graph, int * x_t, const int & out_shape, int * name)
members.summary: Reshape `x_t` to the trace's concrete `out_shape`.
members.extended:
When `x_t` has a symbolic batch (leading dim -1) AND the view keeps the
batch at dim 0, mark dim 0 of the target -1 so MPSGraph INFERS it at runtime
instead of pinning the trace-time batch.  "Keeps the batch at dim 0" is
proven conservatively by `trailing_numel(in) == trailing_numel(out)`: equal
non-leading numel forces `out_dim0 == in_dim0 == batch` (the view only
restructures the non-batch part — flatten, attention head-split / merge,
reduce-squeeze all satisfy this).  MPSGraph allows exactly one inferred (-1)
dim, so the remaining concrete dims determine it uniquely.

Returns **nil** when `x_t` is symbolic-batch but the view does NOT provably
preserve the batch at dim 0 — e.g. `unsqueeze(0)` (batch slides to dim 1) or
a transpose-then-reshape, and also batch-merging views like
`(B,T,E)->(B*T,E)` which we conservatively reject.  Such a view cannot be
represented under a dim-0 symbolic batch, so the caller MUST fall back
(`return false` → per-shape / eager) rather than emit a mis-shaped graph
that would silently produce wrong numerics at non-trace batch sizes.

Static (non-dynamic) compiles are unaffected — `symbolic_batch_at_dim0` is
false, so `out_shape` is used verbatim, identical to the prior behaviour.

members.name: reshape_to_recorded
members.signature: int * reshape_to_recorded(int * g, int * t, const OpNode & node)
members.summary: `t` reshaped to the shape the trace recorded for the node's first output — for an op whose MPSGraph result has no static shape.  nil when the recording has a symbolic axis (the dynamic batch).

members.name: run_executable
members.signature: int run_executable(CompiledExecutable * exe, const int & input_feeds)
members.summary: Run a compiled executable.

parameters.name: exe
parameters.description: Executable returned by `compile_trace`; must be non-null.

parameters.name: input_feeds
parameters.description: Inputs in the executable's `input_ids` order.  Each feed must live on the same device as the executable; the GPU path materialises the underlying `MTLBuffer` via the MLX bridge and binds it as an `MPSGraphTensorData`.

returns.description: Freshly-allocated output tensors in `output_ids` order.  Each output's `GpuStorage` wraps a new `MTLBuffer` allocated by the executable run — no copy back to MLX.

notes:
Implementation lives in `CompiledExecutable.mm` (Objective-C++)
so all MPSGraph types stay in one translation unit.

members.name: run_executable_inplace
members.signature: void run_executable_inplace(CompiledExecutable * exe, const int & input_feeds, const int & output_targets)
members.summary: In-place variant: instead of allocating fresh MTLBuffers per output and returning new TensorImpls, write each output directly into the corresponding pre-existing TensorImpl's GPU buffer.  Used by the compiled-optimizer step path where every output is a parameter (or optimizer-state buffer) that already has an allocated MTLBuffer; skipping the alloc + copy_ round-trip cuts the wrapper's overhead by ~50%.

parameters.name: output_targets
parameters.description: Pre-existing tensors whose elements receive the executable's outputs.  Must equal `output_ids.size() + grad_output_ids.size()` in length, and each target must match its slot's shape and dtype exactly (no broadcasting).  A target may be a Metal view of part of a tensor: its elements are written into its part of the base.

notes:
Not supported in dynamic-batch mode (output shapes vary per call,
no stable target buffers).  Each target's version moves after the
write so autograd's mutation tracker sees the update.  A target whose
buffer is its elements has its MLX array reference replaced with a
fresh one wrapping the output buffer, which also drops any cached MLX
dependency state.

members.name: run_executable_inplace_outputs
members.signature: int run_executable_inplace_outputs(CompiledExecutable * exe, const int & input_feeds, const int & output_targets)
members.summary: Execute `exe` for `run_executable_inplace` and return one fresh `GpuStorage` per slot in `output_targets` (with `arr` null in alias mode), without mutating the targets' storage or versions.  Safe to run with the Python GIL released once feeds have been resolved; follow with `swap_executable_inplace_targets` under the GIL.

members.name: settle_ceil_divisor
members.signature: bool settle_ceil_divisor(const OpNode & node, bool ceil_mode, bool & include_zero_pad)

The reference divides a window hanging past the padded input by the part inside it; MPSGraph, counting the padding, by the whole kernel — no option matches.  Without padding there is nothing to count and the reference's divisor is the in-bounds part, which is MPSGraph's divisor when it does not count the padding.  Returns false when the pairing must stay eager, else settles `include_zero_pad` (ResNeSt's shortcut pool is the unpadded case).

members.summary: Shape accessor that pulls the producer's recorded output shape for `tid` out of the trace.  Used when a VJP needs to know "what shape was input k of this op?" without materialising a forward tensor.

Walks `trace.ops` once looking for the node whose outputs include

produced by any node) — callers must handle that fallback (typically

members.name: shape_to_ns

members.name: shapes_agree_off_axis
members.signature: bool shapes_agree_off_axis(int * a, int * b, int skip_axis)
members.summary: MPSGraph's along-axis gather and scatter want the index to match the data on every axis but `skip_axis` (pass -1 for none).  The reference — and Lucid's eager kernels — allow an index shorter there, and MPSGraph handed one aborted the process: "updates shape and indices shape must match except at axis".  Such a call is declined and runs eagerly.

members.name: complex_abs_forward
members.summary: Autograd node for the element-wise absolute value $y = |x|$.
members.extended:
Saves the input `x` so the backward pass can recover $\mathrm{sign}(x)$
and scale the upstream gradient by it.  The derivative is undefined at
$x = 0$; the implementation follows the reference framework's convention
of returning $0$ there (sub-gradient).

**Math**

$$y = |x|, \qquad
\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = \mathrm{sign}(x), \qquad
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} =
\mathrm{sign}(x)\,\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y}.$$
notes:
Dispatch: Accelerate `vDSP_vabs` (CPU) / MLX `abs` (GPU).
Backward for `abs` of a *complex* input.

The forward is a composite (scale, divide, square, sqrt) chosen to be
overflow-safe, and its derivative cannot be, at exactly zero: the
divide's own backward forms `-re / m^2`, and the clamped `m` is
`FLT_MIN`, whose square underflows to zero in float32.  `0 / 0` is
NaN, so `abs(fft2(x))` came back all-NaN whenever one coefficient of
the transform was zero — which for most real inputs, one is.

Raising the clamp is not available: the trailing multiply uses the
*unclamped* magnitude, so a floor above `|z|` would silently wreck
genuinely tiny inputs.  The derivative is exact and simple enough to
state directly instead:
d|z| / dz = z / |z|,     and 0 at z = 0
which is the subgradient the reference reports there.

members.name: concatenate_op
members.signature: int concatenate_op(const int & xs, int axis)
members.summary: Concatenate a sequence of tensors along an existing axis.
members.extended:
All inputs must share dtype, device, and rank; every dimension except
`axis` must agree exactly.  The output reuses freshly allocated storage —
no input buffer is aliased — and the autograd node saves only per-input
shapes so backward can split the gradient back into one slice per input.

**Math**

$$ y_{[\ldots,\, k,\, \ldots]} = x^{(i)}_{[\ldots,\, k - \sum_{j<i} N_j,\, \ldots]} $$
where $i$ is the unique input index satisfying
$\sum_{j<i} N_j \le k < \sum_{j \le i} N_j$.

**Shape**

Inputs of shape `(D_0, ..., D_{axis-1}, N_i, D_{axis+1}, ..., D_{ndim-1})`
produce output of shape
`(D_0, ..., D_{axis-1}, \sum_i N_i, D_{axis+1}, ..., D_{ndim-1})`.

**See Also**

`stack_op`, `split_op`, `hstack_op`, `vstack_op`.

parameters.name: xs
parameters.description: Non-empty list of input tensors with matching dtype, device, and rank. All dimensions except `axis` must be identical across inputs.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Axis along which to concatenate.  Supports negative indexing (wrapped to `axis + ndim`).  Must satisfy `-ndim <= axis < ndim`.

returns.description: Output tensor of shape `(..., \sum_i N_i, ...)` where the `axis` dimension is the sum of each input's `axis` dimension.

raises.description: If inputs disagree on dtype.
If inputs reside on different devices.
If inputs disagree on any non-concat dimension, or differ in rank.

notes:
Backward slices the incoming gradient back into per-input pieces using the
saved size of each input along `axis`; the schema is
`"concatenate"` with `AmpPolicy::KeepInput`.

members.name: contiguous_op
members.summary: Return a dense, row-major copy of `a` whenever its strides diverge from the canonical contiguous layout; return `a` unchanged when it is already contiguous.
members.extended:
This is the public entry point every CRTP kernel `forward()` calls
on CPU inputs before handing storage to a backend compute routine.
Slices and transposes produce non-unit strides without copying data,
but the Accelerate (CPU) kernels assume stride-1 row-major access, so
materialising a contiguous copy is required to avoid garbage reads.

**See Also**

`ContiguousBackward` — the underlying op implementation.
`UnaryKernel`, `BinaryKernel`, `ReduceKernel` —
CRTP bases that invoke this helper during forward.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Source tensor.  Must be non-null.  May live on either device.

returns.description: Either `a` itself (when `a->is_contiguous()` is true) or a freshly allocated `TensorImpl` with the same shape, dtype, and device but a contiguous storage whose elements are copied from `a` honouring its strides and `storage_offset`.

raises.description: If `a` is null.

notes:
**Autograd.**  Implemented via `ContiguousBackward` so the operation
participates in the autograd graph; the backward is the identity on
the incoming gradient (a clone to give the upstream node an owning
buffer).  See `ops/utils/Contiguous.cpp`.

**GPU path.**  On `Device::GPU` the underlying MLX backend
handles non-contiguous storage natively via lazy evaluation, so the
dispatched `contiguous` is typically a cheap pass-through.  Kernel
`forward()` helpers therefore guard the call with a
`device() == CPU && !is_contiguous()` predicate.

**Aliasing.**  The returned tensor never aliases `a`'s storage when
a copy was performed; consumers may freely mutate it without
violating the version counter on `a`.

members.name: contiguous_stride
members.signature: int contiguous_stride(const int & shape, int elem_size)
members.summary: Computes the row-major (C-contiguous) byte-stride vector for a tensor with the given shape and element size.
members.extended:
The stride is built back-to-front: the innermost (last) axis has stride
`elem_size`, and each outer axis's stride is the product of the inner
stride and the inner dimension size.  This matches NumPy's default
`'C'` order and is the layout expected by Apple Accelerate BLAS / vDSP
routines.

**Math**

$$\text{stride}[i] = \text{elem\_size} \cdot \prod_{j > i} \text{shape}[j]$$

**See Also**

`TensorMeta::is_contiguous_for`
    Reverse check — verifies a stored stride against the canonical one.

parameters.name: shape
parameters.description: A concrete shape.  Empty shape yields an empty stride.

parameters.name: elem_size
parameters.description: Element size in bytes — typically obtained from `dtype_size`.

returns.description: Vector of the same length as `shape`.  When the result is fed back into `TensorMeta`, `TensorImpl::is_contiguous` returns `true`.

raises.description: A dimension is negative (`throw_negative_dim`).  The tensor constructor derives its stride here, so no tensor is built with one.

examples:
contiguous_stride({2, 3, 4}, 4)    // {48, 16, 4}  (float32)
    contiguous_stride({}, 4)           // {}           (scalar)

members.name: conv1d_op
members.signature: int conv1d_op(const int & x, const int & W, const int & b, int stride_l, int pad_l, int dilation_l, int groups)
members.summary: One-dimensional cross-correlation over a batch of signals.
members.extended:
Computes the autograd-aware op
$y[b, c_o, l] = \sum_{c_i, k} x[b, c_i, s\,l + d\,k] \cdot W[c_o, c_i, k] + b[c_o]$
where `s` is the stride and `d` is the dilation.

parameters.name: W
parameters.description: Filters of shape `(C_out, C_in / groups, KL)`.

parameters.name: stride_l
parameters.description: Stride along the length axis.  Default: `1`.

parameters.name: pad_l
parameters.description: Zero-padding added to both ends of `L`.  Default: `0`.

returns.description: Output of shape `(B, C_out, L_out)` where $L_\text{out} = \lfloor (L + 2 p - d(KL - 1) - 1)/s + 1 \rfloor$.

members.name: conv2d_op
members.signature: int conv2d_op(const int & x, const int & W, const int & b, int stride_h, int stride_w, int pad_h, int pad_w, int dilation_h, int dilation_w, int groups)
members.summary: Two-dimensional cross-correlation over a batch of images / feature maps.
members.extended:
Computes
$$
y[b, c_o, h, w] = \sum_{c_i, k_h, k_w}
  x[b, c_i, s_h h + d_h k_h, s_w w + d_w k_w]
  \cdot W[c_o, c_i, k_h, k_w] + b[c_o].
$$

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Input of shape `(B, C_in, H, W)`.

parameters.name: W
parameters.description: Filters of shape `(C_out, C_in / groups, KH, KW)`.

returns.description: Output of shape `(B, C_out, H_out, W_out)` with $H_\text{out} = \lfloor (H + 2 p_h - d_h(KH - 1) - 1)/s_h + 1 \rfloor$ and analogously for $W_\text{out}$.

members.name: conv3d_op
members.signature: int conv3d_op(const int & x, const int & W, const int & b, int stride_d, int stride_h, int stride_w, int pad_d, int pad_h, int pad_w, int dilation_d, int dilation_h, int dilation_w, int groups)
members.summary: Three-dimensional cross-correlation over a batch of volumes.
members.extended:
Performs the natural extension of 2-D convolution to the additional
depth axis `D`, summing the kernel response across
$(k_d, k_h, k_w)$.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Input of shape `(B, C_in, D, H, W)`.

parameters.name: W
parameters.description: Filters of shape `(C_out, C_in / groups, KD, KH, KW)`.

returns.description: Output of shape `(B, C_out, D_out, H_out, W_out)` where each output extent follows $X_\text{out} = \lfloor (X + 2 p_x - d_x(K_X - 1) - 1)/s_x + 1 \rfloor$ for $X \in \{D, H, W\}$.

members.name: conv_transpose1d_op
members.signature: int conv_transpose1d_op(const int & x, const int & W, const int & b, int stride_l, int pad_l, int opad_l, int dilation_l, int groups)
members.summary: One-dimensional transposed convolution (fractionally-strided conv).
members.extended:
Upsamples a 1-D batch by inserting `stride - 1` implicit zeros
between consecutive input positions, then applies a regular
cross-correlation against the kernel.  This is the primitive used in
decoder / generator architectures to lengthen sequences.

parameters.name: W
parameters.description: Filters of shape `(C_in, C_out / groups, KL)`.

parameters.name: pad_l
parameters.description: Length-axis padding subtracted from the output extent. Default: `0`.

parameters.name: opad_l
parameters.description: Length-axis output padding (one-sided).  Must be `< stride_l`. Default: `0`.

returns.description: Output of shape `(B, C_out, L_out)` where $L_\text{out} = (L - 1)\, s - 2 p + KL + p^\text{out}$. dilation_l : int, optional Length-axis spacing between kernel taps.  Default: `1`. groups : int, optional Channel grouping factor.  Default: `1`.

members.name: conv_transpose2d_op
members.signature: int conv_transpose2d_op(const int & x, const int & W, const int & b, int stride_h, int stride_w, int pad_h, int pad_w, int opad_h, int opad_w, int dilation_h, int dilation_w, int groups)
members.summary: Two-dimensional transposed convolution (fractionally-strided conv).
members.extended:
The 2-D upsampling primitive used by VAE / GAN decoders, U-Net
expansion paths, and super-resolution heads.  Equivalent to the
gradient of a 2-D convolution w.r.t. its input.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Input of shape `(B, C_in, H, W)`.

parameters.name: W
parameters.description: Filters of shape `(C_in, C_out / groups, KH, KW)`.

parameters.name: pad_h, pad_w
parameters.description: Per-axis padding subtracted from the output extent. Default: `0`.

returns.description: Output of shape `(B, C_out, H_out, W_out)` with $H_\text{out} = (H - 1) s_h - 2 p_h + KH + p^\text{out}_h$ and analogously for $W_\text{out}$.

notes:
When `stride > 1` and `kernel_size` is not divisible by
`stride` the output can exhibit characteristic *checkerboard*
artefacts.  A common mitigation is to choose
`kernel_size = stride * n` or to substitute bilinear upsampling
followed by a regular convolution.
dilation_h, dilation_w : int, optional
    Per-axis spacing between kernel taps.  Default: `1`.
groups : int, optional
    Channel grouping factor.  Default: `1`.

simultaneously.

returns.description: Output of shape `(B, C_out, D_out, H_out, W_out)` with each output extent following $X_\text{out} = (X - 1) s_x - 2 p_x + K_X + p^\text{out}_x$ for $X \in \{D, H, W\}$. dilation_d, dilation_h, dilation_w : int, optional Per-axis spacing between kernel taps.  Default: `1`. groups : int, optional Channel grouping factor.  Default: `1`.

members.signature: int compute_plan(const int & path, ComputeUnits units)
members.summary: Ask Core ML which device each operation will actually run on.
members.extended:
This exists because the failure it detects is silent.  Requesting
`CpuAndNeuralEngine` on a program the Neural Engine cannot take —
float32 is the common reason — does not warn, does not error, and
returns correct results at CPU speed.  Without this the only evidence
that the accelerator is being used is that the model got faster, which
is not evidence at all.

Backed by `MLComputePlan` (macOS 14.4+).  Returns an empty vector
when the platform is older, which callers must treat as "unknown"
rather than "not accelerated".  `path` is a package, compiled for
the call and removed after it, or a `.mlmodelc`, read in place.
