members.name: inv_op
members.summary: Compute $A^{-1}$ for a square float tensor.
members.extended:
Validates that `a` is at least 2-D, square in the trailing two
axes, and float-typed; dispatches to the backend; and wires
`InvBackward` into the autograd graph (saving only the output)
when grad mode is active.

**Shape**

- `a`: `(..., N, N)`.
- Output: same shape as `a`.

**See Also**

solve_op : Often a better alternative — solves $AX = B$ without
    forming $A^{-1}$ explicitly, with better conditioning.
det_op : Determinant, which uses `inv_op` in its backward.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input matrix of shape `(..., N, N)`.

returns.description: Inverse $A^{-1}$ of identical shape to `a`.

raises.description: If `a` is not square, fewer than 2-D, or non-float.
(At backend level.) If $A$ is singular (LU produces a zero pivot).

members.name: invert_op
members.summary: Element-wise bitwise NOT — returns the bit-flipped tensor with the same integer dtype as `a`.
members.extended:
Not differentiable: output is detached from the autograd graph.

**Math**

$$y_i = \mathtt{\sim} x_i$$

**Shape**

Output shape equals input shape (elementwise).

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input tensor of integer dtype (`Bool`, `Int8`, `Int16`, `Int32`, `Int64`, or unsigned variants).  Floating-point dtypes raise an error.

returns.description: New tensor with the bitwise complement; same shape, dtype, and device as `a`.

raises.annotation: Errors if ``a`` has a floating-point dtype — bitwise NOT is only

notes:
Exposed in Python as both `invert` and `bitwise_not` (reference
framework alias).

members.name: irfftn_op
members.signature: int irfftn_op(const int & a, const int & n, const int & axes)
members.summary: N-dimensional inverse real DFT (complex Hermitian-half to real).
members.extended:
Reconstructs the real signal from a Hermitian-half spectrum produced
by `rfftn`.  The last transformed axis is expanded from the stored
length $n_{\text{last}}/2 + 1$ back to $n_{\text{last}}$.  Uses the
`"backward"` normalisation convention (divides by $\prod_j N_j$).

**Math**

$$
  x[n_1, \dots, n_d] = \frac{1}{\prod_j N_j}
    \sum_{k_1=0}^{N_1-1} \cdots \sum_{k_d=0}^{N_d-1}
    X[k_1, \dots, k_d] \,
    \exp\!\left( +2\pi i \sum_{j=1}^{d} \frac{k_j n_j}{N_j} \right) ,
$$

reconstructed assuming $X$ is Hermitian-symmetric along the last
transformed axis ($X[\dots, N_d - k_d] = \overline{X[\dots, k_d]}$).

**Shape**

`out.shape[axes[i]] == n[i]` when `n` is supplied; otherwise
`out.shape[axes.back()] == 2 * (a.shape[axes.back()] - 1)` and
other transformed axes are unchanged.

**See Also**

rfftn_op : Forward real-input DFT.
ifftn_op : Inverse of full complex-to-complex DFT.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Complex input (C64), shaped as the output of `rfftn`.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Per-axis transform length.  The last entry specifies the original real-input length along `axes.back()`; when `n` is empty, the default `2 * (a.shape[axes.back()] - 1)` is used.

parameters.name: axes
parameters.description: Axes to transform.  Must be non-empty.  Negative values are normalised against the input rank.

returns.description: F32 tensor.  Shape follows `a` except that `axes[i]` is replaced by `n[i]` (with the default applied to the last axis when `n` is empty).

raises.description: If `a` is null, not C64, `axes` is empty, or `len(n) != len(axes)` when `n` is non-empty.

notes:
FFT bypasses IBackend dispatch and calls MLX directly (see
`_Detail.h`).  When the original real length was odd, `n.back()`
must be supplied explicitly — the default formula assumes even length.

members.name: is_anomaly_enabled
members.summary: Read the process-wide autograd anomaly-detection flag.
members.extended:
**See Also**

`set_anomaly_enabled`
`lucid.autograd.detect_anomaly`

returns.description: `true` when backward node outputs should be checked for `NaN` values.

members.name: is_complex
members.summary: Predicate: does the dtype hold a complex pair?
members.extended:
Both complex types answer `true` and neither is floating point under
`is_floating_point`, which is deliberate: their lanes are floats
but they take a separate dispatch, and a real-only kernel handed a
complex buffer would read two elements as one.

returns.description: `true` for `C64` and `C128`.

members.name: is_floating_point
members.summary: Predicate: is the dtype a real floating-point type?
members.extended:
`Dtype::C64` is **not** floating point under this predicate even
though its lanes are float32 — complex tensors take a separate dispatch
path in most kernels.

returns.description: `true` for `F16`, `F32`, `F64`; `false` otherwise.

notes:
Must be kept in sync with the `Dtype` enum: if BF16 is added,
it should be included here.

members.name: is_half_float
members.summary: Predicate: is the dtype one of the two 16-bit float formats?
members.extended:
A property of the dtype, so it lives beside `is_floating_point`
rather than in any one backend.  Accelerate has kernels for neither
format, so both take the same widen-reuse-narrow route through
float32 across the CPU backend — and the random generators, which
have no input to widen, use it to decide to draw wide and round.

returns.description: `true` for `F16` and `BF16`, `false` otherwise.

members.name: is_integral
members.summary: Predicate: is the dtype a signed integer type?
members.extended:
`Dtype::Bool` is intentionally **excluded** — booleans are stored
as 1-byte integers but have no meaningful arithmetic interpretation in
the integer sense, so promotion / index validation paths should not
treat them as integers.

returns.description: `true` for `I8`, `I16`, `I32`, `I64`; `false` for everything else (including `Bool`).

members.name: is_mutation_on_saved_allowed
members.summary: Read the process-wide "allow mutation on saved tensors" flag.
members.extended:
**See Also**

`set_mutation_on_saved_allowed`
`lucid.autograd.graph.allow_mutation_on_saved_tensors`

returns.description: Current state of the override.  When `true`, `check_version_match` becomes a no-op.

members.name: isclose_op
members.signature: int isclose_op(const int & a, const int & b, double rtol, double atol)
members.summary: Elementwise tolerance check: $|a - b| \le \mathrm{atol} + \mathrm{rtol} \cdot |b|$.
members.extended:
Composite over `sub_op` + `abs_op` + `mul_op` +
`add_op` + `less_equal_op` — no dedicated kernel required.
`rtol` and `atol` are materialised as same-shape constant tensors so
the multiply does not depend on any scalar-broadcast support in the
binary ops.  Returns a bool tensor; not differentiable.

**Math**

$$
  y_i = \mathbb{1}\!\left[ |a_i - b_i| \le \mathrm{atol} + \mathrm{rtol} \cdot |b_i| \right]
$$

returns.description: Bool tensor on the broadcast shape of `a` and `b`.

notes:
The asymmetry in `b` matches the reference framework's convention —
swap operands if the symmetric formulation is needed.

members.name: isfinite_op
members.summary: Element-wise test for finite values — returns a boolean tensor that is `True` at every position whose input is neither `NaN` nor $\pm\infty$.
members.extended:
Not differentiable: no autograd node is wired and the result is always
detached.

**Math**

$$y_i = \neg \operatorname{isnan}(x_i) \wedge \neg \operatorname{isinf}(x_i)$$

**Shape**

Output shape equals input shape (elementwise).

**See Also**

`isnan_op`, `isinf_op`.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input tensor of any floating-point dtype.  Integer inputs always produce `True` since every integer value is finite.

returns.description: Boolean tensor with the same shape and device as `a`; dtype is `Dtype::Bool`.

notes:
Equivalent to `~(isnan(a) | isinf(a))` but dispatched as a single
backend kernel for efficiency.

members.name: isinf_op
members.summary: Element-wise test for $\pm\infty$ — returns a boolean tensor that is `True` at every position whose input is positive or negative infinity.
members.extended:
Not differentiable: this op does not register an autograd node, so the
returned tensor is detached even if `a` has `requires_grad=True`.

**Math**

$$y_i = \begin{cases} \text{True} & x_i = +\infty \text{ or } x_i = -\infty \\
                      \text{False} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

**Shape**

Output shape equals input shape (elementwise).

**See Also**

`isnan_op`, `isfinite_op`, `nan_to_num_op`.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input tensor of any floating-point dtype.  Integer dtypes always produce `False` at every position (no value can represent infinity).

returns.description: Boolean tensor with the same shape and device as `a`.  Dtype is `Dtype::Bool` regardless of `a->dtype()`.

notes:
CPU dispatch uses Accelerate's vector isinf primitive; GPU dispatch
uses MLX's `isinf`.  NaN inputs yield `False` (NaN is neither
finite nor infinite).

members.name: isnan_op
members.summary: Element-wise test for `NaN` values — returns a boolean tensor that is `True` at every position whose input is `NaN`.
members.extended:
Not differentiable: returns a detached boolean tensor with no autograd
node, regardless of `a->requires_grad()`.

**Math**

$$y_i = (x_i \ne x_i)$$

The IEEE-754 property "NaN does not equal itself" defines the predicate.

**Shape**

Output shape equals input shape (elementwise).

**See Also**

`isinf_op`, `isfinite_op`, `nan_to_num_op`.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input tensor of any floating-point dtype.  Integer inputs always produce `False` since no integer encodes NaN.

returns.description: Boolean tensor with the same shape and device as `a`; dtype is `Dtype::Bool`.

notes:
Useful as a guard inside composite reductions (`nanmean`, `nansum`)
where NaN-tainted slots must be replaced before accumulation.

members.name: cpu_matmul_nd
members.signature: CpuStorage cpu_matmul_nd(const CpuStorage & a, const CpuStorage & b, const NdMatmulInfo & info, bool transA, bool transB, Dtype dt)
members.summary: Execute a batched N-D matrix multiplication on the CPU.
members.extended:
Iterates over the flattened batch dimension described by `info` and
dispatches one `sgemm` (or `dgemm`) per batch slice via the
Accelerate BLAS wrappers in `backend/cpu/Blas.h`.  Optional transpose
flags reuse the same kernel for the matmul backward pass:
$dA = dOut \cdot B^T$ uses `transB = true` and
$dB = A^T \cdot dOut$ uses `transA = true`.

**Math**

For each batch index $\mathbf{b}$ in `info.out_shape[:-2]`:
$$
  C[\mathbf{b}] = \mathrm{op}_A(A[\mathbf{b}]) \cdot \mathrm{op}_B(B[\mathbf{b}])
$$
where $\mathrm{op}_X(X) = X^T$ if the corresponding transpose flag is
set, else $X$.

**See Also**

backend::cpu::sgemm : Single-precision Accelerate GEMM wrapper.
backend::cpu::dgemm : Double-precision Accelerate GEMM wrapper.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Left operand; logical shape `info.a_bcast_shape`.  Assumed to be pre-broadcast and contiguous in row-major layout.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Right operand; logical shape `info.b_bcast_shape`.  Assumed to be pre-broadcast and contiguous in row-major layout.

parameters.name: transA
parameters.description: If true, treat each $A$ slice as $K \times M$ (transposed) before the GEMM call — adjusts the leading dimension accordingly.

parameters.name: transB
parameters.description: If true, treat each $B$ slice as $N \times K$ (transposed) before the GEMM call.

parameters.name: dt
parameters.description: Element dtype; only `Dtype::F32` and `Dtype::F64` are supported.

returns.description: Newly allocated, aligned output buffer of shape `info.out_shape` (flattened, row-major).  All-zero contraction dims ($M$, $N$, or $K$ equal to 0) yield a zero-filled output.

raises.description: If `dt` is not one of `Dtype::F32` or `Dtype::F64`.

notes:
Leading dimensions are set based on the transpose flags: the
untransposed $M \times K$ slice has `lda = K`, while a transposed
$K \times M$ view has `lda = M`.  The output leading dimension is
always $N$ (untransposed output).

members.name: gather_nd_cpu
members.summary: Gather elements from a source buffer at precomputed flat positions.
members.extended:
Reads `n_out` values from `src_data` at the row-major offsets in
`flat_indices` and writes them sequentially into `dst_data`.  This
is the inner loop of every index-select / embedding-lookup operation:
callers pre-compute the flat index map once and reuse it across the
gather plus the corresponding scatter in the backward pass.

**Math**

For every output position $i$:
$$
  \text{dst}[i] = \text{src}[\text{flat\_indices}[i]]
$$

**See Also**

scatter_add_cpu : The adjoint operation used in the backward pass.

parameters.name: src_data
parameters.description: Pointer to the contiguous source buffer.

parameters.name: dst_data
parameters.description: Pointer to the contiguous destination buffer with at least `n_out` writable elements.

parameters.name: flat_indices
parameters.description: Row-major flat offsets into `src_data`; one entry per output element.  Size must equal `n_out`.

notes:
The caller is responsible for ensuring every index is in-bounds.  The
function performs no bounds checking on release builds — only an
assertion that the index vector length matches `n_out`.

members.name: make_zero_cpu_storage
members.summary: Allocate a new zero-filled CpuStorage.
members.extended:
Convenience constructor used when building gradient accumulation
buffers: allocates an aligned byte buffer sized for `numel` elements
of dtype `dt` and clears it to zero so that subsequent scatter-add
calls accumulate against a clean slate.

**See Also**

zero_cpu_storage : In-place re-zero of an existing storage.
scatter_add_cpu  : Primary consumer of the zero-initialised buffer.

parameters.name: numel
parameters.description: Number of elements (not bytes) to allocate.

parameters.name: dt
parameters.description: Element dtype; determines the per-element byte size via `dtype_size`.

returns.description: Newly allocated, aligned, fully zero-filled storage with `nbytes = numel * dtype_size(dt)`.

members.name: plan_nd_matmul
members.signature: NdMatmulInfo plan_nd_matmul(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Plan an N-D matmul from two operand shapes.
members.extended:
Validates that both operands are at least 2-D, that the inner
contraction dimensions agree, and that the leading batch dimensions
broadcast against each other under NumPy rules.  Returns a fully
populated `NdMatmulInfo` describing the GEMM loop bounds.

**Math**

Splits each operand into a leading batch shape and a trailing matrix
shape, then broadcasts the batch shapes:
$$
  A \in \mathbb{R}^{B_a \times M \times K}, \quad
  B \in \mathbb{R}^{B_b \times K \times N}, \quad
  B_\text{out} = \mathrm{broadcast}(B_a, B_b)
$$
so that the output has shape `out_shape = B_out + [M, N]`.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Shape of the left operand; must satisfy `a.size() >= 2` with trailing dims `[..., M, K]`.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Shape of the right operand; must satisfy `b.size() >= 2` with trailing dims `[..., K, N]`.

returns.description: Plan describing the output shape, per-operand broadcast shapes, contraction dims, and total batch count.

raises.description: If either operand has rank below 2, the inner contraction dimensions disagree, or the leading batch dimensions cannot be broadcast under NumPy rules (a leading dim of 1 expands to match the other operand's value).

notes:
Either operand may have an empty batch shape — in that case the other
operand's batch dims become the output's batch dims unchanged.

members.name: scatter_add_cpu
members.summary: Weighted scatter-add into a destination buffer at scattered positions.
members.extended:
Adjoint of `gather_nd_cpu`: every value of `src` is multiplied
by the corresponding `weights` entry and added into `dst` at the
flat position `flat_dst_indices[i]`.  Duplicate indices accumulate
by summation — the mathematically correct gradient transform whenever
the forward gather read the same source position more than once
(e.g., shared embedding rows, overlapping upsample windows).

**Math**

For each contribution index $i$:
$$
  \text{dst}[\,\text{flat\_dst\_indices}[i]\,]
  \mathrel{+}= \text{src}[i] \cdot \text{weights}[i]
$$
Multiple $i$ mapping to the same destination index sum together.

**See Also**

gather_nd_cpu : The forward gather whose adjoint this implements.
make_zero_cpu_storage : Convenience allocator for a pre-zeroed
    gradient buffer.

parameters.name: dst
parameters.description: Destination buffer.  Must be pre-zeroed by the caller when used to build a fresh gradient — this routine only accumulates.

parameters.name: src
parameters.description: Source values to scatter; one entry per contribution.

parameters.name: flat_dst_indices
parameters.description: Row-major flat offsets into `dst`.  Size must be at least `n_contrib`.

parameters.name: weights
parameters.description: Per-contribution scalar weight (e.g., 1.0 for plain scatter, or interpolation coefficients for bilinear backwards).

parameters.name: n_contrib
parameters.description: Number of (src, index, weight) triplets to apply.

notes:
CPU-only routine — single-threaded, no atomics.  The GPU equivalent
uses MLX's native scatter primitive which performs atomic
accumulation across threads.  `dst` ownership remains with the
caller; this function does not allocate.

members.name: zero_cpu_storage
members.summary: Zero all bytes of a CpuStorage in-place.
members.extended:
Convenience wrapper around `std::memset` that handles the
edge cases of a null pointer or zero-sized buffer.  Used to reset
gradient accumulation buffers between mini-batches or before a
scatter-add pass.

parameters.name: s
parameters.description: Storage to zero.  No-op if `s.ptr` is null or `s.nbytes == 0`.

notes:
Operates on the raw byte buffer regardless of dtype; safe for every
numeric `Dtype` since IEEE-754 zero and integer zero both have
all-zero byte representations.

members.name: kron_op
members.signature: int kron_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Kronecker (block tensor) product over matching ranks.
members.extended:
Composite over `reshape_op` + `mul_op` + `reshape_op`.
Interleaves size-1 placeholders so the multiply broadcasts to a
$2 \cdot \mathrm{ndim}$-rank block tensor; the trailing reshape
collapses each `(sa[i], sb[i])` pair into a single `sa[i] * sb[i]`
axis.  Gradient flows through `ReshapeBackward` and `MulBackward`.

**Math**

For rank-2 operands $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ and
$B \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times q}$:
$$
  (A \otimes B)_{ip + r,\, jq + s} = A_{ij} \, B_{rs}
$$
generalised elementwise to arbitrary equal ranks.

**See Also**

`mul_op`, `reshape_op`.

parameters.name: a, b
parameters.description: Operands sharing the same rank `ndim`.  Shapes need not match dimension-by-dimension.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `(sa[0] * sb[0], ..., sa[-1] * sb[-1])`.

raises.description: If either input is null or the ranks differ.

examples: ``kron`` of two ``(2, 3)`` matrices yields a ``(4, 9)`` matrix.

members.name: kthvalue_op
members.signature: int kthvalue_op(const int & a, int k, int dim, bool keepdim)
members.summary: Pluck the $k$-th smallest element along `dim`.
members.extended:
Composite over `sort_op` + `gather_op` (+ optional
`squeeze_op`).  After sorting `a` ascending along `dim`, we
gather the slice at position `k - 1` to obtain the $k$-th smallest
value.  Not differentiable — the integer-valued index breaks the chain;
gradient is conventionally treated as zero.

**Math**

Let $a^{\uparrow}$ be `a` sorted ascending along `dim`.  Then
$$
  y_{\ldots} = a^{\uparrow}_{\ldots, k - 1, \ldots}
$$

**See Also**

`sort_op` — produces the full sorted view.

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: 1-based rank of the value to return.  Must satisfy `1 <= k <= a.shape[dim]`.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Axis to reduce along.  Negative values wrap modulo `a.ndim`.

parameters.name: keepdim
parameters.description: If `true`, retain a size-1 axis at `dim`; otherwise the axis is squeezed off.

returns.description: Tensor with the same shape as `a` except size 1 (or removed) at `dim`.  Dtype matches `a`.

raises.description: If `a` is null or `k` is outside `[1, a.shape[dim]]`.
If `dim` is out of range.

notes:
Unlike the reference framework's API, this entry point returns only the
value — the matching index can be recovered via `argsort_op` if
required.

members.name: layer_norm_op
members.signature: int layer_norm_op(const int & x, const int & gamma, const int & beta, double eps)
members.summary: Public free-function entry point for Layer Normalization.
members.extended:
Thin wrapper that delegates to `LayerNormBackward::forward`.
This is the symbol the pybind11 binding layer forwards to from
`lucid.nn.functional.layer_norm`.

**See Also**

LayerNormBackward : Autograd node implementing the forward + backward.
rms_norm_op       : Variant that omits mean subtraction.

parameters.name: gamma
parameters.description: Per-element scale; must match the trailing dims of `x`.

returns.description: Normalised output, same shape as `x`.

members.name: ldl_factor_op
members.summary: Compute the LDL$^\top$ factorisation of a symmetric matrix.
members.extended:
Returns the packed factor and the pivot index tensor.  Both follow the
LAPACK `*sytrf` storage convention so they are consumable by
`lucid.linalg.ldl_solve` (which composes triangular solves).  Batched
inputs are supported: leading dimensions are treated as independent
matrices and the factorisation is run on each $N \times N$ slice.

**Math**

$$
  P A P^\top = L D L^\top,
$$
where $P$ is the permutation implied by the pivots, $L$ is unit
lower-triangular, and $D$ is block-diagonal with 1$\times$1 and
2$\times$2 blocks.  The 2$\times$2 blocks are necessary when no
scalar pivot can be chosen without losing numerical stability — this is
what allows the factorisation to handle indefinite $A$.

**Shape**

- `a`           : `(..., N, N)`.
- return `[0]`  : `(..., N, N)`.
- return `[1]`  : `(..., N)`.
- return `[2]`  : `(...)`.

**See Also**

- `cholesky_op` — cheaper alternative when $A$ is SPD.
- `solve_triangular_op` — building block for `ldl_solve`.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Square symmetric matrix of shape `(..., N, N)` with dtype `F32` or `F64`.  The matrix need not be positive definite; only the lower triangle is read.

returns.description: - `[0]` packed factor `LD` of shape `(..., N, N)`, same dtype as `a`.  Strict lower triangle stores $L$ (unit diagonal implicit); diagonal and sub-diagonal entries jointly encode $D$ including 2$\times$2 pivot blocks. - `[1]` pivot tensor of shape `(..., N)`, dtype `I32`, following the LAPACK `ipiv` convention (positive: 1$\times$1 pivot; pair of equal negatives: 2$\times$2 pivot block). - `[2]` `info` of the batch shape `(...)`, dtype `I32`: `sytrf`'s code per matrix — `0`, or the first zero (or NaN) 1$\times$1 block of $D$.

raises.description: If `a` is not at least 2-D, not square, or has a non-float dtype. A singular $D$ completes the factorisation and is reported through `info`, never raised.

notes:
- No autograd node is registered; the outputs are leaves.
- The current `ldl_solve` wrapper in `lucid.linalg` only supports
  1$\times$1 pivots (no 2$\times$2 Bunch-Kaufman block solving yet).

members.name: leaky_mask_storage
members.signature: int leaky_mask_storage(const int & s, double slope, int numel, Dtype dt, Device device)
members.summary: LeakyReLU gradient mask: returns `1` where `s >= 0` else `slope`.

returns.description: New storage suitable for element-wise multiplication into `grad_output`.

members.name: leaky_relu_op
members.signature: int leaky_relu_op(const int & a, double slope)
members.summary: Leaky ReLU $y = x$ if $x > 0$ else $\text{slope} \cdot x$.
members.extended:

LeakyReluBackward : Autograd node implementing the gradient rule.

parameters.name: slope
parameters.description: Negative-side slope; `0.01` is the standard default.

returns.description: Output tensor with the same shape as `a`.

members.name: less_equal_op
members.signature: int less_equal_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Element-wise less-than-or-equal comparison.
members.extended:
Computes `out[i] = (a[i] <= b[i])` and returns the result as a Bool
tensor.

Non-differentiable: no autograd node is registered.

**Math**

$$
  \mathrm{out}[i] = \mathbf{1}\!\left[a[i] \leq b[i]\right].
$$

**References**

NumPy `numpy.less_equal`.

**See Also**

less_op, greater_equal_op

parameters.name: a, b
parameters.description: Operands of identical shape, dtype, and device.

returns.description: Bool tensor with the same shape as the inputs.

raises.description: If the operand shapes, dtypes, or devices differ.

members.name: less_op
members.signature: int less_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Element-wise strict less-than comparison.
members.extended:
Computes `out[i] = (a[i] < b[i])` and returns the result as a Bool
tensor.

Non-differentiable: no autograd node is registered.

**Math**

$$
  \mathrm{out}[i] = \mathbf{1}\!\left[a[i] < b[i]\right].
$$

**References**

NumPy `numpy.less`.

**See Also**

less_equal_op, greater_op

parameters.name: a, b
parameters.description: Operands of identical shape, dtype, and device.

returns.description: Bool tensor with the same shape as the inputs.

raises.description: If the operand shapes, dtypes, or devices differ.

members.name: linear_op
members.signature: int linear_op(const int & x, const int & W, const int & b)
members.summary: Public free-function entry point for the linear op.
members.extended:
Thin wrapper that delegates to `LinearBackward::forward`.  This
is the symbol the pybind11 binding layer (`bind_nn.cpp`) and other
C++ call sites use; calling it directly is equivalent to using the
node's static forward.

**See Also**

LinearBackward : Autograd node implementing the actual forward + backward.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Bias of shape `(N,)` (zero-length tensor when bias is disabled).

returns.description: Output tensor of shape $(\ast, N)$.

members.name: linspace_op
members.signature: int linspace_op(double start, double stop, int num, Dtype dt, Device device, bool requires_grad)
members.summary: Create a 1-D tensor with `num` linearly spaced values from `start` to `stop` inclusive.
members.extended:
**Math**

Element $i$ equals
$\text{start} + i \cdot (\text{stop} - \text{start}) / (\text{num} - 1)$;
the final element is pinned to `stop` exactly to avoid floating-point
drift.

parameters.name: requires_grad
parameters.description: Attach a fresh autograd leaf when true.

returns.description: 1-D tensor of length `num`.

raises.description: If `num < 0`.

members.name: log10_op
members.summary: Base-10 logarithm: $y = \log_{10}(x) = \ln x / \ln 10$.
members.extended:
Composite over `log_op` + `div_op`.  Materialises $\ln 10$
as a same-shape constant so the divide does not need scalar broadcasting.
Gradient flows through `LogBackward` and `DivBackward`.

**Math**

$$
  y = \frac{\ln x}{\ln 10}, \qquad \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{x \ln 10}
$$

**See Also**

`log_op`, `log1p_op`.

returns.description: Tensor of the same shape and dtype as `a`.

notes:
Inherits the precision of the underlying `log_op`; no specialised
base-10 kernel is used.

members.name: log1p_op
members.summary: Natural log of 1 + x: $y = \ln(1 + x)$.
members.extended:
Composite over `add_op` + `log_op`, with a rounding
correction that keeps full relative precision for $|x| \ll 1$.  The
gradient is `LogBackward`'s $1 / (1 + x)$: $+\infty$ at $x = -1$ and
finite below it.

**Math**

$$
  y = \ln(1 + x), \qquad \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{1 + x}
$$

**See Also**

`log_op`, `log10_op`.

returns.description: Tensor of the same shape and dtype as `a`.

members.name: log2_inplace_op
members.summary: In-place base-2 logarithm: writes $\log_2 x$ back into `a`.
members.extended:
**Math**

$$a_i \leftarrow \log_2 a_i$$

**See Also**

`log2_op` — out-of-place counterpart.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Tensor to log in place.  Must be non-null.

returns.description: The same pointer as `a`.

members.name: log2_op
members.summary: Compute $y = \log_2(x)$ element-wise.  Allocates a fresh output of the same shape and dtype as `a` and delegates to `Log2Backward::forward`.
members.extended:
**See Also**

`Log2Backward` — backward node.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input tensor of any shape.  Must be strictly positive.

returns.description: Output tensor of the same shape and dtype.

members.name: log_inplace_op
members.summary: In-place natural logarithm: writes $\ln(x)$ back into `a`.
members.extended:
**Math**

$$a_i \leftarrow \ln(a_i)$$

**See Also**

`log_op` — out-of-place counterpart.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Tensor to log in place.  Must be non-null.  Inputs with $a_i \le 0$ follow the backend's convention (typically NaN / $-\infty$).

returns.description: The same pointer as `a`.

members.name: log_op
members.summary: Compute $y = \ln(x)$ element-wise.  Allocates a fresh output of the same shape and dtype as `a` and delegates to `LogBackward::forward`.
members.extended:
**See Also**

`LogBackward` — backward node.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input tensor of any shape.  Must be strictly positive for finite output; non-positive values produce NaN / $-\infty$.

returns.description: Output tensor of the same shape and dtype.

members.name: log_softmax_op
members.signature: int log_softmax_op(const int & a, int axis)
members.summary: Numerically stable log-softmax $y = x - \mathrm{logsumexp}(x, \text{axis})$.
members.extended:
**See Also**

softmax_op : Probability-domain variant.
LogSoftmaxBackward : Autograd node implementing the gradient rule.

parameters.name: axis

notes:
Prefer `log_softmax_op` followed by `nll_loss` over
`log(softmax_op(...))` followed by `nll_loss` — the former is
numerically stable for very confident logits, the latter is not.

members.name: logaddexp_op
members.signature: int logaddexp_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Numerically-stable $\log(\exp(a) + \exp(b))$ via the max-shift trick.
members.extended:
Composite over `maximum_op` + `sub_op` + `exp_op` +
`add_op` + `log_op`.  Factoring out the per-pair max keeps
the exponent's argument $\le 0$ so the underflow side bears the rounding
error rather than the overflow side.

**Math**

$$
  y = m + \ln\!\left( e^{a - m} + e^{b - m} \right),
  \qquad m = \max(a, b)
$$

**See Also**

`logsumexp_op` — generalised reduction over axes.

returns.description: Tensor on the broadcast shape.

members.name: logical_and_op
members.signature: int logical_and_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Elementwise logical AND: $y_i = [a_i \ne 0] \land [b_i \ne 0]$.
members.extended:
Composite over `not_equal_op` (to coerce each operand to a bool
mask) + `bitwise_and_op`.  Not differentiable — the output is
integral and `bitwise_*` has no backward.

**Math**

$$
  y_i = \mathbb{1}\!\left[ a_i \ne 0 \right] \cdot
        \mathbb{1}\!\left[ b_i \ne 0 \right]
$$

**See Also**

`bitwise_and_op` — bit-level variant on integer inputs.

parameters.name: a, b
parameters.description: Operands of broadcastable shapes and arbitrary numeric dtype.

returns.description: Bool tensor on the broadcast shape of `a` and `b`.

members.name: logical_not_op
members.summary: Elementwise logical NOT: $y_i = [a_i = 0]$.
members.extended:
Composite over `equal_op` against zero — strictly cheaper than the
double-flip `bitwise_not(not_equal(a, 0))` pattern.  Not differentiable.

**Math**

$$
  y_i = \mathbb{1}\!\left[ a_i = 0 \right]
$$

**See Also**

`logical_and_op`, `logical_or_op`.

returns.description: Bool tensor of the same shape as `a`.

members.name: logical_or_op
members.signature: int logical_or_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Elementwise logical OR: $y_i = [a_i \ne 0] \lor [b_i \ne 0]$.
members.extended:
Composite over `not_equal_op` + `bitwise_or_op`.  Not
differentiable.

**Math**

$$
  y_i = \mathbb{1}\!\left[ a_i \ne 0 \,\lor\, b_i \ne 0 \right]
$$

**See Also**

`bitwise_or_op` — bit-level variant on integer inputs.

returns.description: Bool tensor on the broadcast shape.

members.name: logical_xor_op
members.signature: int logical_xor_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Elementwise logical XOR: $y_i = [a_i \ne 0] \oplus [b_i \ne 0]$.
members.extended:
Composite over `not_equal_op` + `bitwise_xor_op`.  Not
differentiable.

**Math**

$$
  y_i = \mathbb{1}\!\left[ (a_i \ne 0) \ne (b_i \ne 0) \right]
$$

**See Also**

`bitwise_xor_op` — bit-level variant.

returns.description: Bool tensor on the broadcast shape.

members.name: logspace_op
members.signature: int logspace_op(double start, double stop, int num, double base, Dtype dt, Device device, bool requires_grad)
members.summary: Create a 1-D tensor of `num` values logarithmically spaced.

members.name: logsumexp_op
members.signature: int logsumexp_op(const int & a, const int & axes, bool keepdims)
members.summary: Numerically-stable $\log \sum_i \exp(x_i)$ via the max-shift trick.
members.extended:
Composite over `max_op` + `sub_op` + `exp_op` +
`sum_op` + `log_op` + `add_op` (+ `squeeze_op`).
Subtracting the per-reduction-group max keeps the largest exponent
argument at $0$ so the rest underflow rather than overflow; the offset
is added back outside the log.  Gradient flows through `MaxBackward`,
`SubBackward`, `ExpBackward`, `SumBackward`, `LogBackward`, and
`AddBackward` automatically — no dedicated backward node is registered.

**Math**

$$
  y = m + \ln \!\left( \sum_{i \in \mathrm{axes}} \exp(x_i - m) \right),
  \qquad m = \max_{i \in \mathrm{axes}} x_i
$$

**See Also**

`logaddexp_op` — two-operand elementwise variant.

parameters.name: axes
parameters.description: Axes to reduce.  Negative values wrap modulo `a.ndim`.  An empty list reduces over all axes per the primitive's convention.

parameters.name: keepdims
parameters.description: If `true`, retain size-1 placeholders at the reduced positions. Otherwise, the reduced axes are squeezed off (in descending order so each remaining index stays valid through the sequential squeeze loop).

returns.description: Reduced tensor.  Dtype matches `a`.

notes:
The intermediate `max_op` is computed with `keepdims=true` so
the broadcast subtract is well defined; the optional axis collapse is
done at the end on the keep-dim result.

members.name: lstm_op
members.signature: int lstm_op(const int & input, const int & h0, const int & c0, const int & weights, const backend::IBackend::LstmOpts & opts)
members.summary: Run a single-layer LSTM forward pass and return `{output, hn, cn}`.
members.extended:
Thin public entry point that delegates to `LstmBackward::forward`
and is bound into Python as `lucid._C.engine.nn.lstm_forward`.  The
Python LSTM module in `lucid.nn.modules.rnn` calls this once per
layer per direction and composes multi-layer, bidirectional and
inter-layer dropout behaviour itself.

**Math**

Per-time-step gating (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber 1997):
$$
  \begin{aligned}
    i_t &= \sigma(W_{ii}\,x_t + W_{hi}\,h_{t-1} + b_i) \\
    f_t &= \sigma(W_{if}\,x_t + W_{hf}\,h_{t-1} + b_f) \\
    g_t &= \tanh(W_{ig}\,x_t + W_{hg}\,h_{t-1} + b_g) \\
    o_t &= \sigma(W_{io}\,x_t + W_{ho}\,h_{t-1} + b_o) \\
    c_t &= f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t,\qquad h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t)
  \end{aligned}
$$

**References**

Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, "Long Short-Term Memory" (Neural Computation
1997).

**See Also**

`lucid.nn.LSTM` — Python multi-layer / bidirectional /
    projection wrapper that composes single-layer engine calls.
`lucid.nn.LSTMCell` — single-time-step variant.

parameters.name: h0
parameters.description: Initial hidden state shaped `(1, B, H_rec)` (zero-filled by the caller if no explicit initial state is supplied).

parameters.name: c0
parameters.description: Initial cell state shaped `(1, B, hidden_size)`.

parameters.name: weights
parameters.description: Layer weights `{W_ih, W_hh, b_ih, b_hh}` (plus optional `W_hr` when projection is enabled).  Gate matrices are stacked in `[i, f, g, o]` order along the leading axis.

returns.description: `{output, hn, cn}` — output sequence `(T, B, H_out)`, final hidden state `(1, B, H_out)`, final cell state `(1, B, hidden_size)`.

notes:
`output`, `hn` and `cn` are all differentiable — see
`LstmBackward`.

members.name: lu_factor_op
members.summary: Compute the LU factorisation $PA = LU$ of a square matrix.
members.extended:
**Shape**

- Input `a`: `(..., n, n)`.
- Output `LU_packed`: `(..., n, n)`.
- Output `pivots`: `(..., n)` with `Dtype::I32`.
- Output `info`: `(...)` with `Dtype::I32`.

**References**

LAPACK `sgetrf`/`dgetrf`; *LAPACK Users' Guide* §2.5.

**See Also**

[[lu_solve_op]] : Apply the factors to solve $Ax = b$.
[[solve_op]]    : End-to-end differentiable linear solve.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Square float tensor of shape `(..., n, n)`.  Leading dimensions are treated as independent batch axes — one factorisation is produced per batch element.

returns.description: A three-element vector `{LU_packed, pivots, info}`: - `LU_packed` has the same shape and dtype as `a`; its upper triangle holds $U$ and its strict lower triangle holds the off-diagonal entries of $L$ (unit diagonal is implicit). - `pivots` has shape `(..., n)` and dtype `I32`; entries are 1-based row indices matching the LAPACK convention. - `info` has the batch shape `(...)` and dtype `I32`: `getrf`'s code per matrix, `0` or the first exactly-zero pivot (1-based).

raises.description: When `a` is below 2-D or not float-typed.  A singular matrix is reported through `info`, never raised.

members.name: lu_solve_op
members.signature: int lu_solve_op(const int & LU, const int & pivots, const int & b)
members.summary: Solve $Ax = b$ given the packed LU factors and pivot vector.
members.extended:
**Shape**

- `LU`: `(*, n, n)`.
- `pivots`: `LU.shape[:-1]`.
- `b`: `(*, n, k)`, or `(n,)` (vector RHS).
- Output: the broadcast batch followed by `(n, k)`, or by `(n,)` for
  a vector RHS.

**References**

LAPACK `sgetrs`/`dgetrs`; *LAPACK Users' Guide* §2.5.1.

**See Also**

[[lu_factor_op]] : Produce the packed factors consumed here.
[[solve_op]]     : Differentiable one-shot solve (factor + apply).

parameters.name: LU
parameters.description: Packed LU matrix of shape `(..., n, n)` as returned by [[lu_factor_op]] — upper triangle holds $U$, strict lower triangle holds the off-diagonal entries of $L$.

parameters.name: pivots
parameters.description: 1-based pivot indices of shape `LU.shape[:-1]` and dtype `I32`.

returns.description: Solution tensor with the dtype of `b`.

raises.description: When `pivots` is not `LU.shape[:-1]` or `b` breaks the right-hand-side contract — before any LAPACK call.
When `LU` or `b` is not a float dtype, or when any argument is null.

members.summary: Extract elements where a boolean mask is true.

Returns a 1-D tensor containing the elements of `a` at the positions
where `mask` is true, in row-major (C) order.  The output length is

positions.

members.name: matmul_op
members.signature: int matmul_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Compute $A B$ with full NumPy-style batch broadcasting and autograd.
members.extended:
Thin public wrapper that delegates to `MatmulBackward::forward`.

**Math**

$$
  C[\ldots, i, j] = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} A[\ldots, i, k]\, B[\ldots, k, j]
$$

**See Also**

dot_op : Rank-1 / rank-2 specialised dispatch.
MatmulBackward : Autograd node implementing the backward pass.

returns.description: Result tensor $C = A B$ with broadcast batch shape and trailing $(M, N)$.

examples:
// C++: 2-D × 2-D plain GEMM.
    auto C = matmul_op(A, B);  // A: [M,K], B: [K,N]  → C: [M,N]
notes:
FLOPs per output element ≈ $2K$; total $\approx 2 \cdot B \cdot M \cdot
N \cdot K$ where $B$ is the broadcast batch size.

members.name: matrix_power_op
members.signature: int matrix_power_op(const int & a, int n)
members.summary: Compute $A^n$ for a square float matrix and integer exponent.
members.extended:
Validates that `a` is at least 2-D, square in the trailing two
axes, and float-typed; dispatches to the backend.  The output
shape always matches `a`'s shape (matrix powers preserve shape).
Autograd is not wired — the result is a leaf in the gradient
graph.

**Math**

$$
  A^n = \begin{cases}
    I & n = 0, \\
    \underbrace{A \cdot A \cdots A}_{n\;\text{times}} & n > 0, \\
    (A^{-1})^{|n|} & n < 0.
  \end{cases}
$$
Repeated squaring decomposes $n = \sum_i b_i 2^i$ (its binary
representation) and accumulates the result in
$O(\log |n|)$ matrix multiplies.

**Shape**

- `a`: `(..., N, N)`.
- Output: same shape as `a`.

**References**

Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 2* §4.6.3
(right-to-left binary exponentiation).
Higham, *Functions of Matrices* (2008), §1.2.

**See Also**

inv_op : Used internally when `n < 0`.
matmul_op : Single-step underlying primitive.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input matrix of shape `(..., N, N)`.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Integer exponent.  Named `n` for parity with the reference framework's `matrix_power(a, n)` signature; the algorithm refers to it as $p$ internally.  May be zero, positive, or negative; negative values require $A$ to be invertible.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `(..., N, N)` holding $A^n$ (and the identity matrix if `n == 0`).

raises.description: If `a` is not square, fewer than 2-D, or non-float.
(At backend level, when `n < 0`.) If $A$ is singular.

notes:
- No backward is registered; `matrix_power` outputs are leaves.
- For graph neural networks $A$ is often an adjacency or
  normalised Laplacian — large `n` is fine because cost grows
  only logarithmically.

members.name: meshgrid_op
members.signature: int meshgrid_op(const int & xs, bool indexing_xy)
members.summary: Build N broadcast coordinate grids from N 1-D input tensors.
members.extended:
Given inputs $x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_{N-1}$ with lengths
$L_0, L_1, \ldots, L_{N-1}$, produces N output tensors all of the same
rank-N shape; the $i$-th output broadcasts $x_i$ across every axis
except its "carry" axis, where it varies.  This is the
multi-dimensional analogue of NumPy's `np.meshgrid`.

**Math**

For `ij` indexing:
$$\mathrm{out}_i[k_0, k_1, \ldots, k_{N-1}] = x_i[k_i]$$

**See Also**

Concat : Stack the resulting grids along a new leading axis.

parameters.name: xs
parameters.description: One or more 1-D input tensors.  All must share the same dtype and device.

parameters.name: indexing_xy
parameters.description: Axis convention for the first two inputs: * `false` — `"ij"` (matrix) indexing.  Output `i` varies along axis `i`; output shape is `(L_0, L_1, ..., L_{N-1})`. * `true` — `"xy"` (Cartesian) indexing.  Output 0 varies along axis 1 (x) and output 1 varies along axis 0 (y); outputs `i >= 2` follow the `ij` convention.  Output shape is `(L_1, L_0, L_2, ..., L_{N-1})`.

returns.description: N coordinate grids, one per input, each of rank N.

examples:
>>> X, Y = meshgrid([x, y], indexing_xy=true)  // 'xy' convention
>>> X.shape == (len(y), len(x))
True
notes:
Backward sums each output gradient over every axis except the carry
axis to recover the gradient w.r.t. the corresponding 1-D input.  All
inputs must be 1-D; mismatched ranks raise.

members.name: mm_op
members.signature: int mm_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Strict 2-D matrix multiply: $C = A \cdot B$.
members.extended:
Composite — rank-checked alias of `matmul_op` that rejects inputs
of rank $\ne 2$ up front so the error message names `mm` rather than
the planner.  Gradient flows through `MatmulBackward`.

**Math**

$$
  C_{ij} = \sum_{k} A_{ik} \, B_{kj}
$$

**See Also**

`matmul_op` — generalised version with broadcasting and 1-D
vector promotion; `bmm_op` — strict batched variant.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `(M, N)`.

raises.description: If either input is null or not exactly 2-D.

members.name: movedim_op
members.signature: int movedim_op(const int & a, const int & source, const int & destination)
members.summary: Move dimensions from `source` to `destination` positions.
members.extended:
Composite over `permute_op`.  Builds an explicit permutation in
which every axis listed in `source` is placed at the matching index in
`destination`; axes not listed preserve their original relative order
and fill the remaining slots left to right.  No new backward node —
gradient flows through `PermuteBackward`.

**Math**

If $\pi$ is the constructed permutation of $[0, n)$, then
$$
  y_{i_0, \ldots, i_{n-1}} = a_{i_{\pi(0)}, \ldots, i_{\pi(n-1)}}
$$

**See Also**

`permute_op` — underlying primitive.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: Axes of `a` to move.  Negative values wrap modulo `a.ndim`. Must be unique.

parameters.name: destination
parameters.description: Target positions for the moved axes, parallel to `source`. Negative values wrap.  Must be unique and have the same length as `source`.

returns.description: A view (or contiguous copy, per the primitive's policy) of `a` with the requested axis order.

raises.description: If `a` is null, the lists differ in length, or either list contains duplicates.
If any axis is out of range.

examples:
``movedim_op(a, {0}, {-1})`` moves the leading axis to the trailing
position — equivalent to a cyclic left rotation of axes.

members.name: nan_to_num_op
members.signature: int nan_to_num_op(const int & a, int nan_val, int posinf_val, int neginf_val)
members.summary: Replace `NaN` and $\pm\infty$ values with user-specified finite substitutes, preserving dtype and shape.
members.extended:
Differentiable: the gradient passes through finite slots and is zero
where a value was replaced (`NanToNumBackward`).

**Math**

$$y_i = \begin{cases}
  \text{nan\_val}    & x_i \text{ is NaN} \\
  \text{posinf\_val} & x_i = +\infty \\
  \text{neginf\_val} & x_i = -\infty \\
  x_i                & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}$$

**Shape**

Output shape equals input shape (elementwise).

**See Also**

`isnan_op`, `isinf_op`, `isfinite_op`.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input tensor of any floating-point dtype.  Integer inputs are passed through unchanged (no non-finite values to replace).

parameters.name: posinf_val
parameters.description: Replacement for $+\infty$ positions.  `nullopt` means the largest finite value of `a`'s dtype (65504 for float16, ~`3.3895e+38` for bfloat16, ~`3.4028e+38` for float32, ~`1.7977e+308` for float64; per part for complex).

parameters.name: neginf_val
parameters.description: Replacement for $-\infty$ positions.  `nullopt` means the lowest finite value of `a`'s dtype.

returns.description: New tensor with the same shape, dtype, and device as `a`; non-finite slots are replaced according to the three scalars.

notes:
The defaults used to be `float32`'s extremes for every dtype.  In
float16 and bfloat16 those round to infinity, so a default call left every
infinity in place.  float64 got `3.4e38` where the reference framework
gives `1.8e308`.  An explicit replacement is rounded into the dtype as
a cast would round it, so one the dtype cannot hold becomes its infinity
(float16 `posinf=1e10` gives `inf`), as in the reference framework.

members.summary: Slice a contiguous window `[start, start + length)` along `dim`.

parameters.name: length

returns.description: Tensor with the same shape as `a` except size `length` along `dim`.  When the window covers the full axis, the input is returned by identity.

raises.description: If `dim` is out of range or the window falls outside `a`.

members.name: norm_op
members.signature: int norm_op(const int & a, double ord, int axis, bool keepdims)
members.summary: Compute the p-norm of a float tensor over the specified axes.
members.extended:
**Math**

$$
  \|A\|_p = \Bigl(\sum_i |a_i|^p\Bigr)^{1/p}.
$$
For $p = 2$ on a matrix this is the Frobenius norm; for $p = 1$ on
a matrix this is the entrywise L1 norm (not the operator 1-norm).

**Shape**

- `a`: arbitrary float shape.
- Output:
    * `axis` empty, `keepdims=false` $\to$ scalar (rank 0).
    * `axis` empty, `keepdims=true` $\to$ all-ones shape of
      the same rank as `a`.
    * Otherwise: rank of `a` minus the number of reduced axes
      (`keepdims=false`) or rank preserved with those axes set
      to 1 (`keepdims=true`).

**See Also**

SVD.h : Underpins operator norms (spectral, nuclear) once exposed.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input tensor (any float dtype, any shape).

parameters.name: ord
parameters.description: Norm order.  `2.0` selects the Frobenius / Euclidean norm $\|A\|_F = \sqrt{\sum a_{ij}^2}$; `1.0` selects the entrywise L1 norm $\|A\|_1 = \sum |a_{ij}|$.  Other values may be forwarded to the backend in the forward pass but have no registered backward.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Axes to reduce.  Empty means a global reduction over every element; negative indices are accepted and normalised.

parameters.name: keepdims
parameters.description: If `true` the reduced axes are retained as size-1 stubs in the output; otherwise they are removed.

returns.description: Reduced norm tensor.

raises.description: If `a` is non-float.
(At backward time.) If `ord` is not 1.0 or 2.0 and a gradient is requested.

notes:
Operator norms (spectral, nuclear, induced 1-/inf-norm) are not yet
dispatched here — they would require SVD and a separate backward.
This op currently covers only the entrywise reductions.

Runs `run(base, index, src, 0)` on the (1,) views and gives a 0-d base its 0-d result back. is attached — this op is inference-only.

members.name: outer_op
members.signature: int outer_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Compute the outer (tensor) product of two 1-D vectors, yielding a 2-D matrix.
members.extended:
The implementation evaluates the outer product as a degenerate GEMM
between reshaped operands: `a[:, None] @ b[None, :]` — i.e. an
$(M, 1) \times (1, N)$ matmul producing an $(M, N)$ result.  On
Accelerate this maps onto `cblas_sger` (rank-1 update) or
`cblas_*gemm`; on the GPU stream it routes through MLX's matmul
primitive.  Autograd is wired through the package-private
`OuterBackward` node, which saves both operands.

**Math**

Forward:
$$
  C_{ij} = a_i\, b_j
$$
Backward (with $G = \partial L/\partial C$):
$$
  \frac{\partial L}{\partial a_i} = \sum_j G_{ij}\, b_j
    = (G\, b)_i, \qquad
  \frac{\partial L}{\partial b_j} = \sum_i G_{ij}\, a_i
    = (a^\top G)_j
$$

**Shape**

- `a.shape == {M}` and `b.shape == {N}`.
- Output shape `{M, N}`.

**References**

NumPy `numpy.outer` (which Lucid mirrors for the 1-D case).

**See Also**

dot_op : 1-D × 1-D inner product (the "dual" of outer).
inner_op : Last-axis contraction.
matmul_op : Generalised matmul with batch broadcasting.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Left operand.  Must be 1-D with length $M$.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Right operand.  Must be 1-D with length $N$.

returns.description: Output matrix of shape $(M, N)$ with $\mathrm{out}[i, j] = a_i\, b_j$.

raises.description: If either input has rank other than 1.

notes:
Schema uses `AmpPolicy::KeepInput` — outer products on integer
vectors are valid and must not be promoted.

members.name: pad_op
members.summary: Pad a tensor on each side of each dimension with a constant fill value.
members.extended:
`pad_width` is a per-dimension list of `(before, after)` widths whose
length must equal `a.rank()`.  The output preserves the input's dtype and
device; newly added elements are filled with `constant`.

**Math**

$$ y_{[i_0, \ldots, i_{n-1}]} =
       \begin{cases}
           x_{[i_0 - b_0, \ldots, i_{n-1} - b_{n-1}]}
               & \text{if } b_d \le i_d < b_d + D_d \text{ for all } d, \\
           c   & \text{otherwise},
       \end{cases} $$
where $b_d$ is the leading pad width, $D_d$ is the input size at axis
$d$, and $c$ is `constant`.

**Shape**

For each dimension $d$:
$$ \text{out.shape}[d] = \text{a.shape}[d] + \text{pad\_width}[d].\text{first}
                         + \text{pad\_width}[d].\text{second}. $$

**See Also**

`concatenate_op` — pad is conceptually concat with constant tensors.

parameters.name: pad_width
parameters.description: One `(before, after)` pair per dimension of `a`.  Both widths must be non-negative.

parameters.name: constant
parameters.description: Fill value for the padded region.  Cast to the input's dtype before storing.

returns.description: Padded tensor with shape `out.shape[d] = a.shape[d] + before_d + after_d`.

raises.description: If any width in `pad_width` is negative.
If `pad_width.size() != a.rank()`.

examples:
Padding a ``(2, 2)`` tensor with ``pad_width = {(1, 0), (0, 2)}`` and
``constant = 0`` yields a ``(3, 4)`` output whose first row and last two
columns are zeros.
notes:
Backward is implemented in the .cpp via `PadBackward` (schema name
`"pad"`, `AmpPolicy::KeepInput`).  It slices the gradient sequentially
per dimension, discarding `pad_width[d].first` leading and
`pad_width[d].second` trailing elements to recover the original input
region.  Only the constant-fill mode is supported here; reflect / replicate
modes live in higher-level Python wrappers.

members.name: pinv_op
members.summary: Compute the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse $A^+$ of a rectangular matrix.
members.extended:
**Shape**

- Input `a`:  `(..., m, n)`.
- Output:       `(..., n, m)`.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input matrix of shape `(..., m, n)` with leading batch dims.  Need not be square or full rank.  Must be at least 2-D and have a floating-point dtype.

returns.description: The pseudoinverse $A^+$ of shape `(..., n, m)` — the last two dimensions are swapped relative to the input.

raises.description: If `a` is null, has a non-floating-point dtype, or has fewer than two dimensions.

examples:
>>> // Solve a tall least-squares system via the pseudoinverse:
>>> auto x_impl = matmul_op(pinv_op(a_impl), b_impl);
notes:
Internally a full reduced SVD is computed; if the caller already has the
SVD on hand, forming $A^+ = V \Sigma^+ U^\top$ manually avoids the
redundant factorisation.

Such a buffer is given a placeholder pointer, which its zero bytes never read.

members.name: promote_and_check_layer_operands
members.signature: int promote_and_check_layer_operands(const OpSchema & schema, const int & x, const int & W, const int & b)
members.summary: Promote `(x, W, b)` under `schema` (linear / conv / conv_transpose) and require all three to share one dtype after any autocast conversion.

members.name: promote_for_schema
members.signature: int promote_for_schema(const OpSchema & schema, const int & a)
members.summary: Cast an input to the dtype its schema asks for.
members.extended:
`UnaryKernel`, `BinaryKernel` and `ReduceKernel` each open with a
`SchemaGuard` and cast to `effective_dtype()`, so every op
built on them inherits both the autocast policy and the integer
promotion that goes with `real_valued` / `ForceFP32`.  An op that
assembles its own forward — softmax, variance, the activations that
need an extra term — has to ask for the same thing, and the ones that
did not computed in the input's own dtype.

For an integer input that is not an approximation of the answer, it is
a different answer: `softmax` of an int32 tensor came back
`[0, 0, 0]` on Metal and `var` came back `0`, both integer-typed
and both silently wrong, while the CPU raised `NotImplementedError`
for the same call.  Every one of those schemas already said the result
was float; nothing was reading it.

`astype_op` rather than `maybe_cast_for_kernel`, for the reason
`BatchNorm` gives: the cast tensor carries an `AstypeBackward`, so
a float input cast under an autocast scope keeps its place in the
graph instead of silently detaching.

parameters.name: schema
parameters.description: The op's schema — supplies the AMP policy and `real_valued`.

returns.description: `a` unchanged when it is already at the effective dtype, otherwise a cast copy.

notes:
The `SchemaGuard` here dies when this returns, so the op's body
runs with autocast still on — unlike a kernel-template op, whose guard
lives as long as its forward.  Harmless while the body calls the backend
directly; a body built from other `*_op` calls has them apply their
own rows (`softplus`).  Holding a guard for the body is LCD-500-E2.

members.name: qr_op
members.summary: Compute the reduced QR factorisation of a float matrix.
members.extended:
Forward calls LAPACK `*geqrf` + `*orgqr` on the CPU stream or
`mlx::core::linalg::qr` on the GPU stream and returns the two
factors as a length-2 vector `{Q, R}`.  Autograd is not wired —
both outputs are leaves in the gradient graph.

**Math**

$$
  A = Q R, \qquad Q^\top Q = I_k, \qquad R = \mathrm{triu}(R).
$$

**Shape**

- `a`: `(..., m, n)`.
- `Q`: `(..., m, k)`, `R`: `(..., k, n)` with
  $k = \min(m, n)$.

**References**

Golub & Van Loan, *Matrix Computations* (4th ed.), Algorithm 5.2.1
(Householder QR).
Walter & Lehmann, "Algorithmic Differentiation of Linear Algebra
Functions" (2010), §3.
Bettale, "Differentiating the QR Decomposition" (2013).

**See Also**

inv_op : Matrix inverse, often composed with QR for least squares.
Lstsq.h : Direct least-squares solver built on top of QR.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input matrix of shape `(..., m, n)`.  Must be at least 2-D and have a floating-point dtype.  Leading dimensions are treated as independent batch dimensions.

returns.description: Length-2 vector `{Q, R}` where - `Q` has shape `(..., m, k)` with $Q^\top Q = I_k$, - `R` has shape `(..., k, n)` and is upper-triangular, and $k = \min(m, n)$.

raises.description: If `a` is fewer than 2 dimensions or has a non-float dtype.

notes:
- Only the reduced ("thin") factorisation is produced; `mode='complete'`
  parity with the reference framework is not currently exposed.
- No backward is registered.  Wrapping `qr_op` inside a graph
  where `Q` or `R` requires gradients will yield leaf tensors.

members.name: reduce_grad_to_shape
members.signature: int reduce_grad_to_shape(const int & grad, const int & grad_shape, const int & target_shape, Dtype dtype, Device device)
members.summary: Reduce `grad` back to `target_shape` by summing over broadcast axes.
members.extended:
Used in the backward pass of any binary op that broadcast one operand
against the other.  The gradient initially has the broadcast (output)
shape; this helper walks the trailing dimensions and sums along any
axis where `target_shape` is size 1 or absent, so the result matches
the original input shape ready to be accumulated into `.grad`.

**Math**

For each output index `i`,

$$
\text{out}[i] = \sum_{j \in \text{broadcast}(i)} \text{grad}[j].
$$

parameters.description: Incoming gradient at the broadcast shape.

parameters.name: target_shape
parameters.description: Original (pre-broadcast) input shape to reduce back to.

returns.description: Storage of shape `target_shape` with broadcast axes summed.

notes: No-op when `grad_shape == target_shape`.

members.name: refuse_phantom_outside_mode
members.signature: void refuse_phantom_outside_mode(const int & s, int what)
members.summary: The contract for a phantom outside phantom mode: it is inert.  Its shape, dtype, device and autograd flags read as any tensor's, and a write into it is absorbed (absorbs_phantom_write), but an op that would read its values or make a new phantom of it — every op does one or the other — refuses here.  A phantom is made only under the mode, so a block's result can never reach real code dressed as a real tensor.  Called where those two things happen, TensorImpl::storage() and TensorImpl::make_view.

members.summary: The one refusal for a phantom tensor's values — a host read (`item`, `tolist`, NumPy, bytes, printing), a data-dependent shape, a write of a phantom into a real tensor, and an op on a phantom outside the mode alike: there are no values to give.  The op stack the error context holds (every op's OpScopeFull pushes its name) says which op asked.

members.name: register_custom_function

    `node` into the autograd graph as `output`'s `grad_fn`,
    materialising `AccumulateGrad` nodes for any leaves that
    need them and recording version counters for in-place mutation
    checks.

**See Also**

`_register_python_backward_node`.

members.name: repeat_op
members.signature: int repeat_op(const int & a, int repeats, int axis)
members.summary: Repeat the contents of a tensor along a single axis.
members.extended:
Produces an output whose `axis` dimension is `repeats` times larger
than the input's; every other dimension is unchanged.  Each element along
`axis` is replicated as a contiguous block of `repeats` copies in the
output (this is interleaved repetition, distinct from `tile_op`).

**Math**

$$ y_{[\ldots, i_a, \ldots]} = x_{[\ldots, \lfloor i_a / r \rfloor, \ldots]} $$
where $r = $ `repeats` and $i_a$ is the index along `axis`.

**Shape**

`out.shape[axis] = a.shape[axis] * repeats`; all other dims unchanged.

**See Also**

`tile_op` — multi-axis tiling; different element ordering.

parameters.description: Number of times to repeat along `axis`.  Must be > 0.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Axis along which to repeat.  Supports negative indexing.

returns.description: Tensor of shape `a.shape` with the `axis` dimension scaled by `repeats`.

notes:
Backward sums the repeated gradient blocks back into the original shape via
`Dispatcher::repeat_backward`.  Schema name `"repeat"`,
`AmpPolicy::KeepInput`.

members.name: rfftn_op
members.signature: int rfftn_op(const int & a, const int & n, const int & axes)
members.summary: N-dimensional real-to-complex DFT.
members.extended:
Computes the DFT of a real signal and stores only the non-redundant
half along the last transformed axis (the Hermitian half).  The
remaining frequencies can be reconstructed by complex conjugation;
this storage convention matches `numpy.fft.rfftn`.

**Math**

For real input $x$,

$$
  X[k_1, \dots, k_d] = \sum_{n_1=0}^{N_1-1} \cdots \sum_{n_d=0}^{N_d-1}
    x[n_1, \dots, n_d] \,
    \exp\!\left( -2\pi i \sum_{j=1}^{d} \frac{k_j n_j}{N_j} \right) ,
$$

stored over $k_d \in \{0, 1, \dots, N_d/2\}$ only (the last axis is
trimmed by Hermitian symmetry; all other axes are stored in full).

**Shape**

Let `L = axes.back()`.  Then `out.shape[L] == n.back() / 2 + 1`
when `n` is supplied, else `a.shape[L] / 2 + 1`.  All other
transformed axes follow `n` (or the input shape).

**See Also**

irfftn_op : Inverse real DFT.
fftn_op : Full complex-to-complex DFT.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Per-axis transform length.  Empty means "use input sizes". When supplied, `len(n) == len(axes)` is required, and the last transformed axis is stored at `n.back() / 2 + 1`.

parameters.name: axes
parameters.description: Axes to transform.  Must be non-empty (rfftn requires at least one axis).  Negative axes are normalised against the input rank.

returns.description: C64 tensor.  Shape matches the input except for the last entry of `axes`, which becomes `(n_last) / 2 + 1` where `n_last` is `n.back()` (or `a.shape[axes.back()]` when `n` is empty).

raises.description: If `a` is null, has a non-real dtype, `axes` is empty, or `len(n) != len(axes)` when `n` is non-empty.

notes:
FFT bypasses IBackend dispatch and calls MLX directly (see
`_Detail.h`).  The Python wrapper must remember the original last
axis size to disambiguate the inverse.

members.name: rk_combine_op
members.signature: int rk_combine_op(const int & y0, const int & ks, const int & coeffs, double dt)
members.summary: Combine Runge-Kutta stage derivatives into a new state in one fused op.
members.extended:
Computes `y0 + dt * sum_i coeffs[i] * ks[i]` element-wise.  Every
explicit Runge-Kutta step is built from this form: a stage input uses the
Butcher row `a_i` as `coeffs`, the final update uses the weights `b`,
and an embedded error estimate uses `b - b*` with `y0` set to a zero
tensor.

The coefficients arrive as host `double` values rather than tensors,
which is deliberate — a tableau lives on the host, so materialising it as
device tensors would force a synchronisation on every stage of every step.
Terms whose coefficient is exactly zero are skipped entirely; strictly
lower-triangular Butcher rows are mostly zeros, so this removes real work
rather than a hypothetical case.

**Math**

$$ y = y_0 + \Delta t \sum_{i} c_i \, k_i $$

**Shape**

All inputs share shape `(D_0, ..., D_{ndim-1})`; the output has that
same shape.  No broadcasting is performed.

**See Also**

`add_op`, `mul_scalar_op`.

parameters.name: y0
parameters.description: Base state.  Defines the output shape, dtype, and device.

parameters.name: ks
parameters.description: Stage derivatives.  May be empty (the result is then a copy of `y0`).  Each entry must match `y0` in shape, dtype, and device.

parameters.name: coeffs
parameters.description: Per-stage weights; must have the same length as `ks`.

parameters.name: dt
parameters.description: Step size multiplying the whole sum.  A negative `dt` integrates backwards in time and is fully supported.

returns.description: Freshly allocated tensor with the same shape, dtype, and device as `y0`.

raises.description: If any `ks[i]` disagrees with `y0` on shape, or if `ks` and `coeffs` differ in length.
If any `ks[i]` has a different dtype from `y0`.
If any `ks[i]` resides on a different device from `y0`.

notes:
Backward is exact and cheap: the incoming gradient passes straight through
to `y0` and is scaled by `dt * coeffs[i]` for each `ks[i]`.  Keeping
a real backward is what lets a solver be differentiated end-to-end
(discretise-then-optimise); a fused forward without it would silently cut
the graph.  Schema name `"rk_combine"`, `AmpPolicy::Promote` (matching
`add`), deterministic, variadic input arity.

Non-contiguous inputs are materialised through `contiguous_op`
before the arithmetic, so views integrate without a caller-side copy.

members.name: rk_error_norm_op
members.signature: double rk_error_norm_op(const int & y0, const int & y1, const int & ks, const int & coeffs, double dt, double rtol, double atol)
members.summary: Root-mean-square ratio of an embedded error estimate to its tolerance.
members.extended:
Computes, in a single pass and without materialising the error tensor:

err_i   = dt * sum_j coeffs[j] * ks[j][i]
    tol_i   = atol + rtol * max(|y0_i|, |y1_i|)
    result  = sqrt( mean_i( (err_i / tol_i)^2 ) )

The adaptive controller accepts a step when the result is at most 1 and
otherwise retries with a smaller one, so this scalar is read on the host
every single step.  Written as a chain of ordinary tensor ops it would cost
roughly eight passes over the state plus several temporaries and still end
in the same host read; fused it costs one pass, no temporary, one read.

**See Also**

`rk_combine_op` — the fused stage combination this pairs with.

parameters.name: y0
parameters.description: State at the start of the step.  Defines shape, dtype, and device.

parameters.name: y1
parameters.description: Proposed state at the end of the step.

parameters.name: ks
parameters.description: Stage derivatives of the step.  May be empty, in which case the error estimate is identically zero and the result is `0`.

parameters.name: coeffs
parameters.description: Embedded-error weights (`b - b_hat`), one per entry of `ks`.

parameters.name: dt
parameters.description: Step size.  Negative for backwards integration; only the magnitude of the resulting error matters.

parameters.name: rtol, atol
parameters.description: Relative and absolute tolerances.  Both must be non-negative and not both zero, otherwise the tolerance is zero and the ratio is infinite.

returns.description: The error ratio, on the host.  Never negative; `0` when `ks` is empty or every coefficient is zero.

raises.description: If `y1` or any `ks[i]` disagrees with `y0` on shape, or if `ks` and `coeffs` differ in length.
If the operands disagree on dtype.
If the operands reside on different devices.
If the dtype is not `F32` or `F64`.  Step control is a scalar diagnostic, so the Python layer promotes lower-precision states before calling rather than the kernel carrying a half-precision path.

notes:
Not differentiable, by construction — step-size control is a control-flow
decision, not part of the value the caller differentiates.  Returning a
host `double` rather than a tensor makes that structural instead of a
convention someone could accidentally violate.

The accumulation is performed in `double` on the CPU path regardless of
storage dtype, so a large state does not lose the small contributions that
decide whether a step is accepted.

members.signature: int run_slot_hooks(Node & producer, int output_nr, int grad)
members.summary: Run the hooks of output `output_nr` of `producer` on that slot's whole gradient, then retain the result if the tensor asked for it.
members.extended:
The hooks run with the GIL held and grad mode off.  A hook that returned a
tensor replaces the gradient — after the checks `Tensor.grad =` makes —
and one that returned `None` leaves it as the hook left it, in-place
writes included.  Once a hook has run, a CPU gradient is copied before it
flows on: the hook may keep what it was handed, or hand back a tensor
somebody else reads, and the engine adds into gradients in place.

raises.description: A hook raised; the exception reaches the caller of backward as it was.
A hook returned something that is neither a tensor nor `None`.
A hook returned a gradient of another kind than it was given.
