members.name: scaled_dot_product_attention_op
members.signature: int scaled_dot_product_attention_op(const int & q, const int & k, const int & v, const int & attn_mask_or_null, double scale, bool is_causal)
members.summary: Run scaled dot-product attention and return only the output tensor.
members.extended:
Public entry point that wires Lucid's autograd system to the SDPA
kernel.  Internally calls `ScaledDotProductAttentionBackward::forward`
and, when `GradMode::is_enabled()` and any of `q`, `k`, `v`
require a gradient, attaches a fresh `ScaledDotProductAttentionBackward`
node so the output participates in BPTT.

**Math**

$\text{Attn}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right)V$.

**References**

Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need" (NeurIPS 2017).

**See Also**

scaled_dot_product_attention_with_weights_op : Variant that also
    returns the post-softmax attention weight matrix `W`.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Query tensor of shape `(..., L_q, d_k)`.

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Key tensor of shape `(..., L_k, d_k)`.

parameters.name: v
parameters.description: Value tensor of shape `(..., L_k, d_v)`.

parameters.name: attn_mask_or_null
parameters.description: Optional additive mask broadcastable to `(..., L_q, L_k)`; `nullptr` skips the additive term entirely.

parameters.name: scale
parameters.description: Multiplicative factor applied to $QK^\top$ before the softmax.

parameters.name: is_causal
parameters.description: If `true`, an engine-side upper-triangular `-inf` mask is added so each query position attends only to earlier keys.

returns.description: Output tensor of shape `(..., L_q, d_v)`.

members.name: scaled_dot_product_attention_with_weights_op
members.signature: int scaled_dot_product_attention_with_weights_op(const int & q, const int & k, const int & v, const int & attn_mask_or_null, double scale, bool is_causal)
members.summary: Run scaled dot-product attention and return `{output, weights}`.
members.extended:
Identical numerics to `scaled_dot_product_attention_op` but exposes
the post-softmax attention weight matrix
$W = \text{softmax}(QK^\top \cdot s + M)$ shaped `(..., L_q, L_k)`
as a second return value.  Useful for visualisation, head analysis,
or any caller that needs to inspect or further process attention
scores.

When autograd is required, two `ScaledDotProductAttentionBackward`
nodes are wired — one for the output tensor (the normal SDPA
backward) and a second, independent node attached to the weights
tensor so callers may use the weights in downstream loss terms
without conflating gradients between the two outputs.

**See Also**

scaled_dot_product_attention_op : Lighter variant returning only the
    contracted output, when attention weights are not needed.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Query tensor of shape `(..., L_q, d_k)`.

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Key tensor of shape `(..., L_k, d_k)`.

parameters.name: v
parameters.description: Value tensor of shape `(..., L_k, d_v)`.

parameters.name: attn_mask_or_null
parameters.description: Optional additive mask broadcastable to `(..., L_q, L_k)`.

parameters.name: scale
parameters.description: Multiplicative factor applied to $QK^\top$ before the softmax.

parameters.name: is_causal
parameters.description: If `true`, an upper-triangular `-inf` mask is applied engine-side.

returns.description: A two-element vector `{output, weights}` where `output` has shape `(..., L_q, d_v)` and `weights` has shape `(..., L_q, L_k)`.

notes:
On the MLX (GPU) path the fused kernel does not produce a dense
weight matrix; this entry point therefore recomputes
$\text{softmax}(QK^\top \cdot s + M)$ to materialise the weights for
the caller.  On the Accelerate (CPU) path the weight matrix is a
natural byproduct of the manual softmax and is returned directly.

members.name: scatter_add_op
members.signature: int scatter_add_op(const int & base, const int & indices, const int & src, int dim)
members.summary: User-facing scatter-add: `out = base` with `src` accumulated at positions given by `indices` along `dim`.
members.extended:
**Math**

$$
  \text{out}[i_0, \dots, i_{d-1}, \text{indices}[j], i_{d+1}, \dots]
  \mathrel{+}= \text{src}[i_0, \dots, j, \dots]
$$

parameters.name: base
parameters.description: Tensor providing the initial values; same shape as the output.

parameters.name: indices
parameters.description: int32 or int64 tensor indexing into `base` along `dim`.  Shape matches `src`.

returns.description: Same shape and dtype as `base`.

raises.description: If `src` is not in `base`'s dtype or `indices` is not int32 / int64 — the rule of `scatter_amax_op`, `scatter_amin_op`, `scatter_prod_op` and `scatter_set_op` too.  Nothing is cast.

notes:
Full autograd support.  Gradients: $\partial / \partial \text{base} = \text{grad\_out}$,
$\partial / \partial \text{src} = \text{gather}(\text{grad\_out}, \text{dim}, \text{indices})$.

members.name: scatter_amax_op
members.signature: int scatter_amax_op(const int & base, const int & indices, const int & src, int dim)
members.summary: Scatter with element-wise `max` reduction at duplicate indices.
members.extended:
**Math**

At each output slot $i$, the result is the maximum among `base[i]`
and all `src[j]` with `indices[j] == i`.

**See Also**

scatter_amin_op : Same pattern with `min` reduction.

returns.description: Reduced tensor, same shape and dtype as `base`.

notes:
Backward flows only through "winning" elements:
  $\partial / \partial \text{src}[j] = \text{grad}[\text{idx}[j]]$ when $\text{src}[j] = \text{out}[\text{idx}[j]]$, else $0$;
  $\partial / \partial \text{base}[i] = \text{grad}[i]$ when $\text{base}[i] = \text{out}[i]$, else $0$.
Ties distribute the gradient equally to all winners (matches the
reference framework).

members.name: scatter_amin_op
members.signature: int scatter_amin_op(const int & base, const int & indices, const int & src, int dim)
members.summary: Scatter with element-wise `min` reduction at duplicate indices.
members.extended:
**Math**

At each output slot $i$, the result is the minimum among `base[i]`
and all `src[j]` with `indices[j] == i`.

**See Also**

scatter_amax_op : Companion `max` variant.

returns.description: Reduced tensor, same shape and dtype as `base`.

notes:
Backward identical to `scatter_amax_op` with the winner predicate
flipped to "matches the output minimum".

members.name: scatter_op
members.signature: int scatter_op(const int & base, int dim, const int & indices, const int & src)
members.summary: Overwrite-semantics scatter: $\mathrm{out}[..., \mathrm{idx}, ...] = \mathrm{src}$.
members.extended:
A true overwrite on the backend's `scatter_set` kernel, every dtype —
what `x[key] = v` and `lucid.scatter` run.  It was a scatter-add of the
delta $\mathrm{src} - \mathrm{base}[\mathrm{idx}]$, which is not one: NaN
or inf in `base` survived the write, a tiny value rounded away against a
large one, bool could not become False, and a repeated index summed.

**Math**

$$
  y_i = \begin{cases}
    \mathrm{src}_j & \text{if } i = \mathrm{idx}_j \text{ for some } j \\
    \mathrm{base}_i & \text{otherwise}
  \end{cases}
$$

**See Also**

`scatter_add_op` — additive variant.
`scatter_set_op` — `index_copy`'s stricter-shaped entry to this op.

parameters.name: base
parameters.description: Tensor to scatter into.  Provides the output shape and dtype.

parameters.name: indices
parameters.description: Integer tensor (`int32` or `int64`) of `base`'s rank, no larger than `src` on any axis nor than `base` on any but `dim`.

parameters.name: src
parameters.description: Source values written into `base` at the positions given by `indices`; only the corner the index covers is read.  Cast to `base`'s dtype first.

returns.description: A new tensor with the same shape and dtype as `base`.

raises.description: If any input is null, `indices` is not an integer dtype, or the shapes break the rule above.
If `dim` is out of range, or (CPU) an index is.

notes:
A position named more than once keeps the value written last on the CPU,
where each line along `dim` is written in index order — the reference's
CPU behaviour.  On Metal the writes race and which value survives is
unspecified, as on the reference's GPU backends.  int64 and complex64
scatter through the CPU on Metal (MLX has no 8-byte scatter there).

Backward, the reference's rule: `base` takes the gradient with the
written positions zeroed, `src` the gradient gathered from where each
element landed — every duplicate included.  Differentiable twice.

members.name: scatter_prod_op
members.signature: int scatter_prod_op(const int & base, const int & indices, const int & src, int dim)
members.summary: Scatter with multiplicative reduction.
members.extended:
**Math**

$$
  \text{out}[i] = \text{base}[i] \cdot \prod_{j : \text{idx}[j] = i} \text{src}[j] .
$$

returns.description: Same shape and dtype as `base`.

notes:
Each operand's gradient is `grad` at its position times the product of
the other operands there — `out / operand` where the operand is not
zero, and computed without that division where it is, so a zero operand
gets the others' product rather than NaN.

members.name: scatter_set_op
members.signature: int scatter_set_op(const int & base, const int & indices, const int & src, int dim)
members.summary: scatter_set: out[..., index[i], ...] = src[..., i, ...] along dim (overwrite). A copy of `base` with the indexed slices replaced by `src` — the single-op primitive that `index_copy` routes through.

returns.description: Same shape and dtype as `base`.

notes:
Gradients:
  $\partial / \partial \text{base}[i] = \text{grad}[i]$ except at overwritten
  positions where it is 0; $\partial / \partial \text{src}[j] =
  \text{grad}[\text{idx}[j]]$ (a plain gather).  Duplicate indices follow the
  reference framework's last-writer-wins convention.

members.name: schema_hash
members.summary: Computes a 64-bit FNV-1a fingerprint of an op's behavioural schema.
members.extended:
The hash mixes the schema's `name`, `version`, the op's autocast
policy on each device (its row in the policy table, Metal then CPU), and
the `deterministic` flag — what together defines how the op behaves.
`stable_input_indices`, `internal`, and arity counts are excluded
because they describe shape rather than semantics.

Used for change-detection: cached graph compilations, profiler entries,
and checkpoint metadata embed this hash so a schema bump (or any
behaviour-relevant change) invalidates the cache automatically.

**Math**

$$ h_0 = \text{0xcbf29ce484222325}, \qquad
   h_{i+1} = (h_i \oplus b_i) \cdot \text{0x100000001b3} \pmod{2^{64}}, $$

where $b_i$ ranges over the bytes of `name`, a null separator,
the little-endian bytes of `version`, the Metal and CPU policy bytes,
and finally the `deterministic` flag (0 or 1).

returns.description: A 64-bit FNV-1a digest.  Stable across processes for the same schema fields; not cryptographic.

notes:
The null byte between `name` and `version` prevents length-
extension collisions of the form `"ab"` vs `"a" + 'b'`.

members.name: searchsorted_op
members.signature: int searchsorted_op(const int & sorted_1d, const int & values, bool right)
members.summary: Per-query insertion point into a sorted 1-D (or row-wise N-D) reference.
members.extended:
Evaluates each query via binary search in $O(\log N)$ time and $O(1)$
auxiliary memory per query, ordering `NaN` after `+inf` to match the
reference.  Not differentiable — integer output.

**Math**

Let $s$ be the sorted reference and $v$ the query tensor.  Then
$$
  y_{\ldots, j} = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1}
  \mathbb{1}\!\left[ s_i \prec v_{\ldots, j} \right]
$$
with $\prec$ being $<$ when `right = false` (leftmost insertion) and
$\le$ when `right = true` (rightmost insertion).

**See Also**

`bucketize_op` — same operation with the argument order flipped.

parameters.name: sorted_1d
parameters.description: 1-D ascending-sorted reference of length $N$, or an N-D tensor whose leading $N - 1$ dimensions match `values`.

parameters.name: right
parameters.description: If `true`, returns the rightmost (post-equal) insertion point; otherwise the leftmost.

returns.description: `int64` tensor of shape `S` whose entries lie in $[0, N]$.

raises.description: If either input is null or the shapes are incompatible.

members.name: solve_op
members.signature: int solve_op(const int & a, const int & b)
members.summary: Solve the linear system $AX = B$ for $X$.
members.extended:
**Shape**

- `a`: `(*, N, N)`.
- `b`: `(*, N, K)`, `(N,)`, or `a.shape[:-1]` (vector RHS).
- Output: the broadcast batch followed by `(N, K)`, or by `(N,)` for
  a vector RHS.

**References**

[Giles, "Collected Matrix Derivative Results" (Oxford, 2008)](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/gilesm/files/NA-08-01.pdf), §2.4.
LAPACK `sgesv`/`dgesv`; *LAPACK Users' Guide* §2.5.

**See Also**

[[lu_factor_op]] : Standalone LU factorisation (no autograd).
[[lu_solve_op]]  : Apply pre-computed LU factors.
[[matmul_op]]    : Used in the backward outer product $-dB\, X^\top$.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Square float tensor of shape `(..., N, N)`.  Must share dtype and device with `b`.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Right-hand side of shape `(..., N)` or `(..., N, K)`.

returns.description: Solution tensor $X = A^{-1} B$ with the same shape as `b`. When grad mode is active, the result has [[SolveBackward]] wired into the autograd graph with $A$ saved as input and $X$ saved as output.

raises.description: When `b` is none of the shapes above, or the batch axes of `a` and `b` do not broadcast — before any backend call.
When `a` is not square, not float-typed, when dtypes/devices mismatch between `a` and `b`, or when $A$ is singular (zero pivot detected by LU).

examples: Single RHS solve::
auto x = solve_op(a, b);  // a: (n, n), b: (n,) → x: (n,)
Batched multi-RHS solve::
auto x = solve_op(a, b);  // a: (B, n, n), b: (B, n, k)

members.name: solve_triangular_op
members.signature: int solve_triangular_op(const int & a, const int & b, bool upper, bool unitriangular)
members.summary: Solve $A X = B$ for $X$ where $A$ is triangular.
members.extended:
Performs a single substitution sweep through $A$; no factorisation is
required.  $A$ and $B$ must share the same dtype and device.  The batch
axes of $A$ and $B$ broadcast; the backend then runs BLAS once per
aligned slice.

**Math**

Solves
$$
  A X = B \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X = A^{-1} B,
$$
without ever forming $A^{-1}$.  When `unitriangular` is set, $A$ is
regarded as $\widetilde{A}$ with $\widetilde{A}_{ii} = 1$ for all $i$.
The corresponding reverse-mode rule is
$$
  \frac{\partial B}{\partial L} = A^{-\top} \frac{\partial X}{\partial L},
  \qquad
  \frac{\partial A}{\partial L} = -\,\frac{\partial B}{\partial L}\,X^\top,
$$
implemented by [[SolveTriangularBackward]].

**Shape**

- `a` : `(*, N, N)`.
- `b` : `(*, N, K)`, or `(N,)` (vector RHS).
- return: the broadcast batch followed by `(N, K)`, or by `(N,)` for
  a vector RHS.

**See Also**

- `solve_op` — full LU-based dense solve; use when $A$ is not known to
  be triangular.
- `cholesky_op` / `ldl_factor_op` — produce the triangular factors
  this op back-substitutes through.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Triangular coefficient matrix of shape `(..., N, N)` with dtype `F32` or `F64`.  Only the half indicated by `upper` is read.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Right-hand side of shape `(..., N, K)` (or `(..., N)` for a single RHS), same dtype and device as `a`.

parameters.name: upper
parameters.description: If `true` (default), `a` is interpreted as upper-triangular and back-substitution is used.  If `false`, `a` is lower-triangular and forward-substitution is used.

parameters.name: unitriangular
parameters.description: If `true`, the diagonal of `a` is treated as all-ones regardless of its stored values.  Useful for the unit-lower factor produced by LDL$^\top$ and for Householder products.  Default is `false`.

returns.description: Solution $X$ with the dtype of `b` (shape below).

raises.description: If `b` breaks the right-hand-side contract above — before any backend call.
If `a` is not square, if `a` and `b` have mismatched dtype or device, or if either tensor has a non-float dtype.

raises.annotation: $\pm\infty$ / NaN where substitution divided by a zero pivot.

members.name: sort_op
members.signature: int sort_op(const int & a, int axis)
members.summary: Sort a tensor along a single axis in ascending order.
members.extended:
Returns the sorted values; the permutation indices are computed
internally and consumed by the backward pass but are not exposed here.
See `argsort_op` for the indices alone, or `topk_op` for a
(values, indices) pair.

**Math**

Let $\sigma$ be the permutation that sorts `a` along `axis`.  Then
$$y_i = a_{\sigma(i)}, \qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial a_i} =
    \left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial y}\right)_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}.$$

returns.description: Sorted tensor of the same shape and dtype as `a`.

notes:
Differentiable for F32 / F64 inputs only via `IndexScatterBackward`,
which scatters the incoming gradient back to the original positions.
Integer dtypes return a detached output.

members.name: split_at_op
members.signature: int split_at_op(const int & a, int indices, int axis)
members.summary: Split a tensor at user-specified indices along an axis.

consecutive differences between `0`, the sorted `indices`, and

**See Also**

parameters.name: indices
parameters.description: Strictly increasing split positions in the range `[0, a.shape[axis]]`.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Axis to split along.  Supports negative indexing.

returns.description: `indices.size() + 1` tensors whose `axis` dimensions partition `a.shape[axis]`.

members.name: split_op
members.signature: int split_op(const int & a, int num_splits, int axis)
members.summary: Split a tensor into a fixed number of equal pieces along an axis.
members.extended:
The size of `a` along `axis` must be divisible by `num_splits`.
Each output piece is wired with a `SplitSliceBackward` node that

members.name: stack_op
members.signature: int stack_op(const int & xs, int axis)
members.summary: Stack a list of same-shape tensors along a new axis.
members.extended:
Inserts a fresh size-`len(xs)` dimension at position `axis` of the
output, increasing the rank by one.  All inputs must have identical shape,
dtype, and device.

**Shape**

Inputs of shape `(D_0, ..., D_{ndim-1})` stacked along `axis = k` yield
output shape `(D_0, ..., D_{k-1}, len(xs), D_k, ..., D_{ndim-1})`.

**See Also**

`concatenate_op`, `unbind_op`.

parameters.name: xs
parameters.description: Non-empty list of tensors with identical shape, dtype, and device.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Insertion position for the new dimension.  Supports negative indexing against the output rank `ndim + 1` (so `axis = -1` appends).

returns.description: Output tensor with rank `ndim + 1` and a new dimension of size `len(xs)` inserted at `axis`.

raises.description: On any disagreement between inputs.

notes:
Backward slices each size-1 hyperplane along the new axis and squeezes it
to recover the gradient for the corresponding input.  Schema name
`"stack"`, `AmpPolicy::KeepInput`.

members.name: std_op
members.signature: int std_op(const int & a, const int & axes, bool keepdims)
members.summary: Compute the (biased) standard deviation along `axes`.
members.extended:
Defined as $\mathrm{std}(x) = \sqrt{\mathrm{var}(x, \text{axes},
\text{keepdims})}$, where the underlying variance uses the **biased**
estimator $\frac{1}{N}\sum (x - \bar{x})^2$.  No new backward node
is needed: the gradient flows naturally through `SqrtBackward` and
`VarBackward` via the chain rule.

**Math**

$$
  \mathrm{std}(x) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i \in \text{axes}}
  (x_i - \bar{x})^2}.
$$

**See Also**

`var_op` — variance the standard deviation is built on.

parameters.name: axes
parameters.description: Axes to reduce.  Negative indices wrap.

parameters.name: keepdims
parameters.description: If `true`, retains reduced dims as size-1.

returns.description: Output tensor of the reduced shape.

members.name: overlaps_itself
members.signature: bool overlaps_itself(const int & shape, const int & stride)
members.summary: Whether two of a view's elements are the same byte.  A zero stride on an axis longer than one — an expanded view — always makes one; so do windows that overlap, as an unfold with step < size gives, though every stride is non-zero.  Such a view reads fine, and a write into it has no single value for a repeated element to take — unless it is a fill (refuse_ambiguous_write).

members.name: pack
members.signature: void pack(const int * src, int * dst, const int & shape, const int & stride, int elem)
members.summary: Packs a strided view into `dst`, dense and row-major.  `src` points at the view's first element.
members.extended:
This walked every element recursively with a memcpy each — 4.6 ms to
make a 1024 x 1024 float transpose contiguous, where copying the same
bytes takes 0.08 — and every CPU op that reads a view comes through here.
Now the axes are merged first, and the innermost run moves as a memcpy
when it is contiguous, a fill when it is broadcast, and a typed strided
loop otherwise; a view that merges to a 2-D transpose is copied in tiles,
so both sides stay in cache.

members.name: scatter
members.signature: void scatter(const int * packed, int * first, const int & shape, const int & stride, int elem)
members.summary: Lays `packed` — `shape`'s elements, dense and row-major — into the view at `first` through `stride`: the inverse of `pack`.  Runs move as a memcpy when the inner axis is contiguous and as typed stores otherwise.  The view must not repeat an element (`overlaps_itself`).

members.name: with_element_type
members.summary: One element of `elem` bytes as an unsigned integer of that width, so a run moves by typed loads and stores rather than a memcpy per element.

members.signature: int svd_op(const int & a, bool compute_uv)
members.summary: Compute the reduced singular value decomposition of a rectangular matrix.
members.extended:
**Shape**

- Input `a`: `(..., m, n)`.
- `U`:  `(..., m, k)` — left singular vectors as columns.
- `S`:  `(..., k)`    — singular values in descending order.
- `Vh`: `(..., k, n)` — right singular vectors as rows (note: `Vh`
  is $V^\top$, not $V$, matching NumPy/reference-framework convention).

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input matrix of shape `(..., m, n)` with leading batch dims.  Must be at least 2-D and have a floating-point dtype.

parameters.name: compute_uv
parameters.description: When `true` (default) returns the full reduced factorisation $\{U, \Sigma, V^\top\}$.  When `false` returns $\{\Sigma\}$ only, which lets the backend skip assembly of the singular vectors — roughly 2x faster and used by `svdvals` / `matrix_rank` / `cond`.

returns.description: If `compute_uv=true`: `{U, S, Vh}` with $U$ shape `(..., m, k)`, $S$ shape `(..., k)`, $V^\top$ shape `(..., k, n)`, $k = \min(m, n)$. If `compute_uv=false`: `{S}` only.

raises.description: If `a` is null, has dtype that is not floating point, or has fewer than two dimensions.

notes:
Singular values are guaranteed non-negative and sorted in descending
order on output.  Outputs are leaf nodes in the autograd graph at the
C++ level — the Python wrapper attaches the gradient functions.

members.signature: int tensor_from_python(int obj, const int & what)
members.summary: The tensor a Python value holds — a `TensorImpl`, or a `lucid.Tensor` through its `impl` — or null for `None`.  The one Python → TensorImpl conversion of the autograd layer.

raises.description: `obj` is anything else; the message names `what`, the value's role ("a tensor hook's result", ...).

members.name: tensor_hook_runner
members.signature: int tensor_hook_runner(const int & t, const int & make)
members.summary: The runner of `t`'s hooks, installed from `make()` the first time.
members.extended:
A leaf's slot is its own; a non-leaf's is its producer's output slot, so
every consumer — made before the hook or after — sends its gradient through
it.  `t`'s shape is recorded with it.

raises.description: `t` does not require grad, so no gradient will ever reach it.

notes:
A non-leaf's runner lives on its producer for as long as the node does.
The engine drops it once `backward(retain_graph=False)` has released the
node's saved state (`Node::release_tensor_hooks`) — the node can never
run again, and dropping it breaks the cycle tensor → node → runner → hook
closure → tensor that Python's collector cannot see through the engine.
Two consequences the caller should know:

* a hook registered on the output of a node that was *already* released
  that way is installed but never fires (any further backward through the
  node is refused), and it keeps that cycle until the node itself goes;
* a node that saved nothing for backward is never released, so a hook on
  its output that refers to the output keeps the cycle while the graph
  lives — as does a hook on a graph that never runs backward at all.

A leaf's runner lives in its own AutogradMeta, so a leaf hook that refers
to the leaf keeps the leaf alive the same way.  The Python side
(CHA-151-A) should hold the tensor weakly in its runner.

members.name: tensordot_op
members.signature: int tensordot_op(const int & a, const int & b, int axes_a, int axes_b)
members.summary: General multi-axis tensor contraction (NumPy `tensordot`).
members.extended:
Sums the product of `a` and `b` over the axes named pairwise by
`axes_a` and `axes_b`, leaving every other axis as an outer-product
dimension in the output.  This is the multi-axis generalisation of
matrix multiplication: `tensordot(a, b, [k], [0])` over rank-2 inputs
is exactly `a @ b`.

When gradient tracking is active the contraction is lowered to an
equivalent `einsum` string and the einsum backward node handles the
gradient computation, so this op itself does not register a dedicated
backward node.  On the CPU inference path the call is fused into a
permute-reshape-then-scalar-GEMM kernel; on GPU it dispatches to the
MLX `tensordot` primitive.

**Math**

With `axes = (axes_a, axes_b)` and `a`, `b` reshaped into
matrices $A' \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times K}$ and $B' \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N}$
(free dims flattened to $M$ and $N$, contracted dims flattened to $K$),
$$
  C' = A' B', \qquad C = \mathrm{reshape}(C', \text{free}_a + \text{free}_b).
$$
Gradients flow back as two `matmul`-equivalent contractions:
$$
  \frac{\partial L}{\partial A'} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial C'} {B'}^{\top}, \qquad
  \frac{\partial L}{\partial B'} = {A'}^{\top} \frac{\partial L}{\partial C'}.
$$

**Shape**

Let `N = len(axes_a) = len(axes_b)`.  Then
$$
  \mathrm{ndim}(\text{out}) = \mathrm{ndim}(a) + \mathrm{ndim}(b) - 2N.
$$
The contracted-dim sizes must match pairwise:
`a.shape[axes_a[i]] == b.shape[axes_b[i]]` for all `i`.

**References**

NumPy `numpy.tensordot` semantics.

**See Also**

einsum_op, matmul_op

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Left operand.  Any rank, any floating dtype.  `a->dtype()` defines the result dtype.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Right operand.  Must share dtype and device with `a`.

parameters.name: axes_a
parameters.description: Axis indices of `a` to contract over.  Negative indices count from the right and are normalised to `[0, a.ndim)`.

parameters.name: axes_b
parameters.description: Axis indices of `b` to contract over, paired element-wise with `axes_a`.  Must have the same length as `axes_a`.

returns.description: Output of shape `a.shape[free_a] ++ b.shape[free_b]` where `free_*` denotes the axes of each operand that are NOT contracted. The output `ndim` equals `a.ndim + b.ndim - 2 * len(axes_a)`.

raises.description: If `axes_a.size() != axes_b.size()`, if any axis is out of range after normalisation, if a paired pair of axes has mismatched sizes, or if the CPU dtype is neither `F32` nor `F64`.

examples:
Contract the trailing axis of ``a`` with the leading axis of ``b``
(a rank-3 by rank-3 contraction equivalent to ``a @ b`` over the last
two axes when both are 2-D):

auto a = randn({4, 5, 6});  // shape (4, 5, 6)
    auto b = randn({6, 7, 8});  // shape (6, 7, 8)
    auto c = tensordot_op(a, b, {2}, {0});  // shape (4, 5, 7, 8)
Two-axis contraction (full inner product over the trailing pair):

auto a = randn({3, 4, 5});           // shape (3, 4, 5)
    auto b = randn({4, 5, 7});           // shape (4, 5, 7)
    auto c = tensordot_op(a, b, {1, 2}, {0, 1});  // shape (3, 7)
notes:
* `axes_a` and `axes_b` are passed by value so the implementation
  may normalise negative indices in place.
* Inputs need not be contiguous; the CPU path materialises a permuted
  contiguous copy before the GEMM step.
* Saves both inputs and the axes specification (under the einsum
  lowering) for backward.

attributes.name: schema
attributes.description: `"tensordot"`, `AmpPolicy::Promote`.  Lowers to `einsum` when autograd is active.

members.name: cpu_available
members.summary: Whether the CPU backend is available — always `true` in tests.
members.extended:
Provided as a counterpart to `gpu_available` so dtype-parameterised
fixtures can branch on device availability uniformly.  The CPU backend
(Accelerate / vDSP) is always present on the supported Apple Silicon
platforms targeted by Lucid, so this function unconditionally returns
`true`.

**See Also**

`gpu_available`.

returns.description: Always `true`.

members.name: cpu_eye
members.summary: Create an `N \times N` identity matrix on CPU.
members.extended:
Thin wrapper over `eye_op` that produces a square identity with
the main diagonal set to `1` and all off-diagonal entries set to
`0`.  Used in linear-algebra tests as a multiplicative identity
(`A @ I == A`) or as a reference matrix.

**Math**

$$ I_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & i = j \\ 0 & i \ne j \end{cases} $$

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Side length of the square identity matrix.  The resulting tensor has shape `(n, n)`.

returns.description: Newly allocated `(n, n)` CPU tensor with `1` on the main diagonal and `0` elsewhere.

members.name: cpu_full
members.signature: int cpu_full(const int & shape, double value, Dtype dtype)
members.summary: Create a CPU tensor filled with a constant scalar value.
members.extended:
Thin wrapper over `full_op` pinned to `Device::CPU` and
`requires_grad = false`.  The fill value is accepted as `double`
and cast down to `dtype` by the backend kernel.

**See Also**

`cpu_zeros`, `cpu_ones`.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Scalar value broadcast to every element.  Cast to `dtype` during fill.

returns.description: Newly allocated CPU tensor with all elements equal to `value` (after dtype cast).

examples: .. code-block:: cpp

auto x = cpu_full({4}, 2.0);          // [2, 2, 2, 2] F32
    auto y = cpu_full({3}, -1.0, Dtype::F64);

members.name: cpu_ones
members.signature: int cpu_ones(const int & shape, Dtype dtype)
members.summary: Create a CPU tensor filled with ones.
members.extended:
Thin wrapper over `ones_op` pinned to `Device::CPU` and
`requires_grad = false`.  Useful as a multiplicative identity input
or for tests that need a non-zero baseline.

**See Also**

`cpu_zeros`, `cpu_full`.

returns.description: Newly allocated CPU tensor with all elements set to `1`.

members.name: cpu_zeros
members.signature: int cpu_zeros(const int & shape, Dtype dtype)
members.summary: Create a CPU tensor filled with zeros.
members.extended:
Thin wrapper over `zeros_op` pinned to `Device::CPU` and
`requires_grad = false` — the canonical "blank tensor" used as
fixture input for unit tests.

**See Also**

`cpu_ones`, `cpu_full`.

parameters.name: shape
parameters.description: Target tensor shape.  Empty shape produces a 0-dim scalar.

returns.description: Newly allocated CPU tensor of the given shape, with all elements set to `0`.

examples: .. code-block:: cpp

auto x = cpu_zeros({3, 4});                  // F32 by default
    auto y = cpu_zeros({2}, Dtype::F64);         // double precision

members.name: gpu_available
members.summary: Whether the GPU backend (MLX / Metal) is available on the current host.
members.extended:
Probes `backend::Dispatcher::for_device` with
`Device::GPU` and reports success / failure as a boolean.  A
runtime probe (rather than a compile-time constant) is required
because Lucid tests may be cross-compiled or run on machines without
a functioning Metal device.

**See Also**

`cpu_available`.

returns.description: `true` if a GPU dispatcher can be constructed, `false` otherwise (no Metal device, missing MLX initialisation, etc.).

notes:
Catches every exception raised by the dispatcher lookup; treat the
negative result as advisory and skip GPU-only tests via
`GTEST_SKIP()` when this returns `false`.

members.name: grad_numel
members.summary: Number of elements stored in the tensor's gradient buffer.
members.extended:
Derived from `CpuStorage::nbytes` divided by
`dtype_size(t->dtype())`.  Returns `0` when no gradient has
been accumulated — same sentinel as a genuinely empty gradient, so
pair with `has_grad` when the distinction matters.

**See Also**

`has_grad`, `grad_to_float_vec`.

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: The tensor whose gradient size is queried.

returns.description: Element count of the gradient buffer (`nbytes / dtype_size`), or `0` if the tensor has no gradient.

members.name: grad_to_float_vec
members.summary: Extract a tensor's accumulated gradient as a flat `std::vector<float>`.
members.extended:
Mirror of `to_float_vec` but reads from
`TensorImpl::grad_storage` instead of `TensorImpl::storage`.
Returns an empty vector when no gradient has been accumulated — the
caller is responsible for distinguishing that from a genuinely
zero-length gradient via `has_grad` if needed.

**See Also**

`has_grad`, `grad_numel`, `to_float_vec`.

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: The tensor whose gradient is read.  Must have already been touched by `Engine::backward` (verify with `has_grad`).

returns.description: Flat `float` view of the gradient buffer in row-major order. `F64` gradient storage is cast down element-wise.  Empty vector if the tensor has no gradient yet.

notes:
Assumes the gradient lives on the CPU (the normal `Engine::backward`
path).  GPU-resident gradients would need an explicit
`IBackend::to_cpu` transfer that this helper does *not* perform
— extend the helper if your test exercises that path.

members.name: has_grad
members.summary: Whether the tensor currently holds a populated gradient buffer.
members.extended:
Thin predicate over `TensorImpl::grad_storage` — returns
`true` once `Engine::backward` has accumulated into `t`,
`false` for any tensor that has never received a backward signal
(including freshly constructed `requires_grad = true` tensors
before the first backward pass).

**See Also**

`grad_to_float_vec`, `grad_numel`.

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: Any tensor.  Need not have `requires_grad = true`.

returns.description: `true` if `t->grad_storage().has_value()`, `false` otherwise.

members.name: to_float_vec
members.summary: Extract a `TensorImpl` 's raw bytes as a flat `std::vector<float>` for numeric inspection in unit tests.
members.extended:
For CPU tensors, reinterprets the `CpuStorage` buffer directly
— zero copy.  For GPU tensors, performs a one-shot
`IBackend::to_cpu` transfer then reads.  Always returns the
"as-if F32" view, casting from the tensor's native dtype as needed
so the caller can compare without dtype branching.

**See Also**

`grad_to_float_vec`, `EXPECT_TENSOR_NEAR`.

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: The tensor to flatten.  Any shape, any device, dtype `F32` or `F64`.

returns.description: Length equals `t->numel()`.  Elements are in row-major order matching the tensor's logical layout.  `F64` storage is cast down element-wise to `float`.

notes:
Test-only — production code never round-trips GPU→CPU just to read
values.  Use `Storage` accessors or the public
`Tensor::numpy` bridge instead.

The F64 → F32 narrowing is lossy by design: the matcher tolerance
(`tol` parameters on the assertion macros) is expected to absorb
the rounding noise.

members.name: throw_negative_dim
members.summary: Refuses a shape with a negative extent.
members.extended:
Raises `InvalidArgument` naming the innermost op on the error-context
stack and the first negative extent, in the reference framework's words:
`zeros: Trying to create tensor with negative dimension -3: [2, -3]`.
Defined out of line, in `ErrorBuilder.cpp`: the op name lives on
`ErrorContext`, whose header includes this one.  Not exported: only
the engine itself calls it.

members.name: tile_op
members.signature: int tile_op(const int & a, int reps)
members.summary: Tile a tensor by repeating it along multiple axes.
members.extended:
`reps[d]` specifies how many times to repeat along dimension `d`.  If
`reps` is longer than `a.rank()`, the input is conceptually left-padded
with size-1 dimensions before tiling, so the output rank equals
`reps.size()`.

**Math**

$$ y_{[i_0, \ldots, i_{r-1}]} = x_{[i_0 \bmod D_0, \ldots, i_{r-1} \bmod D_{r-1}]} $$
where $D_d$ is the input's effective size along dimension $d$.

**Shape**

Let `r = reps.size()` and `n = a.rank()`.  After left-padding `a` with
`max(r - n, 0)` size-1 dims:
`out.shape[d] = a_padded.shape[d] * reps[d]` for `d in [0, max(r, n))`.

**See Also**

`repeat_op` — single-axis, interleaved variant.

parameters.name: reps
parameters.description: Per-dimension repetition counts.  Each entry must be >= 1.  If `reps.size() > a.rank()`, leading size-1 axes are virtually prepended to the input.

returns.description: Tiled tensor with rank `max(reps.size(), a.rank())` and `out.shape[d] = a_padded.shape[d] * reps[d]`.

notes:
Backward sums the tiled gradient blocks via `Dispatcher::tile_backward`,
which uses the padded input shape and the repetition counts to locate each
contribution.  Schema name `"tile"`, `AmpPolicy::KeepInput`.

members.name: to_device_op
members.signature: int to_device_op(const int & a, Device target)
members.summary: Defined in ops/ufunc/ToDevice.cpp.  Declared here so binary/ternary ops can promote a 0-d CPU scalar operand to the peer's device while keeping the ToDeviceBackward edge on the autograd graph.

members.name: topk_op
members.signature: int topk_op(const int & a, int k, int axis)
members.summary: Top-k values and their indices along an axis.
members.extended:
Selects the `k` largest elements along `axis` and returns them
together with their positions in the original tensor.

**See Also**

sort_op : Full sort (no truncation).
argsort_op : Sort indices only.

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Number of top elements to return.  Must satisfy `0 < k <= a.shape[axis]`.

returns.description: `[values, indices]` where both have shape equal to `a.shape` with `axis` reduced to `k`.  `values` has the dtype of `a`; `indices` has dtype I64.

notes:
`values` is differentiable for F32 / F64 inputs via
`IndexScatterBackward`, which scatters the incoming gradient back to
the selected positions in the original tensor.  `indices` is never
differentiable.

members.name: trace_op
members.summary: Compute the trace (sum of main-diagonal elements) of a matrix or a batch of matrices.
members.extended:
For a 2-D input `a` of shape `[m, n]` the result is a scalar
$\mathrm{tr}(a) = \sum_i a_{ii}$ where $i$ ranges over
$\min(m, n)$.  For a higher-rank input of shape
`[b_0, ..., b_{k-1}, m, n]` the last two dimensions are
contracted: each $[m, n]$ slice produces one scalar, and the result
has shape `[b_0, ..., b_{k-1}]`.

Backward (2-D only) scatters $\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial y$ to
each diagonal position of a zero-filled matrix of the same shape
as `a`:
$\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial a_{ij} =
\mathbb{1}[i = j]\cdot \partial \mathcal{L}/\partial y$.
For batched inputs (`ndim > 2`) the output is returned without an
autograd edge — attempts to backpropagate through batched
`trace_op` will silently produce no gradient.

**Math**

2-D forward and backward:
$$
  y = \sum_{i} a_{ii}, \qquad
  \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a_{ij}} =
  \mathbb{1}[i = j]\cdot
  \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y}.
$$

Batched forward (no offset, no autograd):
$$
  y_{b_0 \dots b_{k-1}} = \sum_{i}
  a_{b_0 \dots b_{k-1}, i, i}.
$$

**Shape**

- Input  `[m, n]`                          → output `[]`
- Input  `[b_0, ..., b_{k-1}, m, n]`       → output
  `[b_0, ..., b_{k-1}]`

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input tensor of any dtype, with `ndim >= 2`.  Non-null.

returns.description: Scalar (`[]`) for 2-D inputs, or a tensor of shape `a.shape[2:]` for batched inputs.

raises.description: If `a` is null or has `ndim < 2`.

notes:
Diagonal offset (analogous to NumPy's `trace(offset=...)`) is not
currently exposed; only the main diagonal is summed.  Autograd is
wired only when `ndim == 2` — the batched path returns a plain
non-differentiable tensor by design.

members.name: transpose_op
members.summary: Reverse all axes of `a`: equivalent to `permute(a, [ndim-1, …, 1, 0])`.
members.extended:
**See Also**

T_op : Alias used to implement the `.T` property.
mT_op : Batch-matrix-transpose variant that only swaps the last two
    axes.

returns.description: View of `a` with reversed axis order.

members.name: tril_op
members.signature: int tril_op(const int & a, int k)
members.summary: Lower-triangular part of a matrix (or batch of matrices).
members.extended:
Zeros every element strictly above the `k`-th diagonal of the last
two axes of `a`.  The main diagonal is `k = 0`; positive `k`
shifts the diagonal toward the upper-right (keeping more elements);
negative `k` toward the lower-left (keeping fewer).

**Math**

$$\mathrm{out}_{\ldots,i,j} = \begin{cases}
    a_{\ldots,i,j} & \text{if } j - i \le k \\
    0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}$$

**See Also**

triu_op : Upper-triangular counterpart.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input tensor of rank $\ge 2$.  The mask is applied to the trailing two axes; leading axes are treated as batch dimensions.

returns.description: Tensor of the same shape and dtype as `a` with the upper triangle (relative to `k`) zeroed.

notes:
Backward applies `tril` with the same `k` to the incoming gradient,
preserving only the gradient at positions retained in the forward pass.

members.name: triu_op
members.signature: int triu_op(const int & a, int k)
members.summary: Upper-triangular part of a matrix (or batch of matrices).
members.extended:
Zeros every element strictly below the `k`-th diagonal of the last
two axes of `a`.  Diagonal offset convention matches `tril_op`.

**Math**

$$\mathrm{out}_{\ldots,i,j} = \begin{cases}
    a_{\ldots,i,j} & \text{if } j - i \ge k \\
    0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}$$

**See Also**

tril_op : Lower-triangular counterpart.

returns.description: Tensor of the same shape and dtype as `a` with the lower triangle (relative to `k`) zeroed.

notes: Backward applies `triu` with the same `k` to the incoming gradient.

members.name: trunc_op
members.summary: Element-wise truncation toward zero; same shape, dtype and device as `a`. Differentiable with a zero gradient, as the reference keeps it.
members.extended:
**See Also**

`floor_op`, `ceil_op`, `frac_op`.

members.name: unbind_op
members.signature: int unbind_op(const int & a, int axis)
members.summary: Unbind a tensor into a list of slices along an axis, dropping that axis.
members.extended:
Produces `a.shape[axis]` tensors, each with rank `ndim - 1`.  The
k-th output is `a[..., k, ...]` along `axis` with the split dimension
squeezed away.

**See Also**

`stack_op` (the inverse), `split_op`.

parameters.name: axis
parameters.description: Axis to unbind along.  Supports negative indexing.

returns.description: `a.shape[axis]` tensors of rank `ndim - 1`.

notes:
Backward inserts the gradient slice back at offset `k` along `axis`
(after unsqueezing) before scattering into the input gradient.

members.name: unflatten_op
members.signature: int unflatten_op(const int & a, int dim, const int & sizes)
members.summary: Inverse of `flatten` — split `dim` into `sizes`.
members.extended:
Composite over `reshape_op`.  The product of `sizes` must equal
`a.shape[dim]`; the surrounding axes are preserved verbatim.  Pure
view operation when the input is contiguous; gradient flows through
`ReshapeBackward`.

**Math**

Let `a` have shape $(s_0, \ldots, s_{d-1}, s_d, s_{d+1}, \ldots)$ and
`sizes` $= (m_0, \ldots, m_{k-1})$ with $\prod_i m_i = s_d$.  Then the
output has shape
$$
  (s_0, \ldots, s_{d-1}, m_0, \ldots, m_{k-1}, s_{d+1}, \ldots)
$$

**See Also**

`reshape_op` — the underlying primitive operates on the full shape.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Axis to expand.  Negative values wrap modulo `a.ndim`.

parameters.name: sizes
parameters.description: Replacement extents.  Their product must equal `a.shape[dim]`.

returns.description: Reshaped tensor whose total `numel` matches `a`.

raises.description: If `a` is null or $\prod \mathrm{sizes} \ne \mathrm{a.shape}[\mathrm{dim}]$.
If `dim` is out of range.

members.name: unfold_dim_op
members.signature: int unfold_dim_op(const int & a, int dim, int size, int step)
members.summary: Sliding-window view of `a` along a single dimension.
members.extended:
**Shape**

Adds a trailing `size`-sized axis; the original `dim` is replaced
by the number of windows `L`.

returns.description: Tensor whose shape is `(*in_shape[:dim], L, *in_shape[dim+1:], size)` where $L = \lfloor (\text{in\_shape}[\text{dim}] - \text{size}) / \text{step} \rfloor + 1$.

notes:
Behaves as a view; backward passes through a `gather` that
accumulates overlapping windows back into the input.

members.name: unfold_op
members.signature: int unfold_op(const int & x, const int & kernel, const int & stride, const int & pad, const int & dilation)
members.summary: Public entry point for Unfold (im2col).
members.extended:
Functional wrapper around `UnfoldBackward::forward` for building
custom convolution-like ops in user code.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Input of shape `(B, C, S_0, ..., S_{N-1})`.

returns.description: Patch-as-columns tensor of shape `(B, C * prod(K), prod(O))`.

members.name: uniform_op
members.signature: int uniform_op(const int & shape, double low, double high, Dtype dt, Device device, Generator * gen)
members.summary: Allocates a tensor filled with uniform samples on $[\mathrm{low}, \mathrm{high})$.
members.extended:
**Math**

$$x_i \sim \mathcal{U}(\mathrm{low}, \mathrm{high})$$

**See Also**

`rand_op` — convenience shortcut for $[0, 1)$.

parameters.name: low
parameters.description: Inclusive lower bound of the support.

parameters.name: high
parameters.description: Exclusive upper bound of the support.  Must be strictly greater than `low`.

parameters.name: gen
parameters.description: Bit-stream state; falls back to `default_generator` on `nullptr`.

returns.description: Newly allocated leaf tensor (`requires_grad = false`).

raises.description: If `high <= low` — surfaced as `ValueError` on the Python side.

members.name: unique_op
members.summary: Unique sorted elements of a tensor.
members.extended:
Flattens `a`, removes duplicates, and returns the result sorted in
ascending order as a 1-D tensor.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input tensor.  Supported dtypes: F32, F64, I32, I64.

returns.description: 1-D tensor of the same dtype as `a` containing the unique elements in sorted order.  Always resides on `Device::CPU` because the output length is data-dependent.

notes: Non-differentiable.

members.name: unsqueeze_op
members.signature: int unsqueeze_op(const int & a, int dim)
members.summary: Insert a new size-1 dimension at a given position.
members.extended:
The new axis is added before position `dim` in the output, so the output
rank is `ndim + 1`.  Negative `dim` wraps relative to the output rank
(so `dim = -1` inserts before the last existing dimension).

**See Also**

`squeeze_op`, `reshape_op`.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Insertion position.  Must satisfy `-(ndim + 1) <= dim <= ndim`.

returns.description: A view with rank `ndim + 1` and a size-1 dimension inserted at `dim`.

raises.description: If `dim` is out of range.

examples:
A length-5 1-D tensor unsqueezed at ``dim=0`` becomes a ``(1, 5)`` view;
unsqueezed at ``dim=1`` becomes a ``(5, 1)`` view.

members.name: var_op
members.signature: int var_op(const int & a, const int & axes, bool keepdims)
members.summary: Compute the biased variance of `a` along `axes`.
members.extended:
Uses the population estimator
$\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2$ — i.e. the
denominator is $N$, not $N - 1$.  This corresponds to the reference
framework's `unbiased=False` (population) variant; the unbiased /
sample variant is not exposed by this entry point.  The standard
deviation `std_op` is built directly on top by composing
`sqrt` with this op so the autograd chain is automatic.

During the forward pass the mean is computed once with
`keepdims=true` and broadcast to the full input shape so that
`VarBackward::apply` can compute $x - \bar{x}$ without a second
broadcast call.  Both the input `x` and the broadcast mean are
saved on the backward node.

**Math**

$$
  \sigma^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i \in \text{axes}}
  (x_i - \bar{x})^2, \qquad
  \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_i} =
  \frac{2}{N}(x_i - \bar{x})\cdot
  \mathrm{broadcast}\!\left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}
  {\partial \sigma^2}\right).
$$

**Shape**

If `keepdims` is `false`, the reduced axes are removed; if
`true`, they become size-$1$.

**See Also**

`std_op` — square root of the variance.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Input tensor of float dtype.  Non-null.

parameters.name: axes
parameters.description: Axes to reduce.  May be empty (reduce all axes).  Negative indices wrap around `ndim`.

parameters.name: keepdims
parameters.description: If `true`, retains reduced dims as size-1 entries; otherwise they are collapsed.

returns.description: Output tensor with the reduced shape.  Autograd is wired when `a->requires_grad()` is true and `GradMode` is enabled.

notes:
Internal dispatch: `IBackend::variance` — Accelerate on CPU, MLX
on GPU.  The CPU implementation uses Welford-style accumulation for
numerical stability on large $N$.  The empty-axis edge case
(`reduced == 0`) clamps the count to $1$ to avoid a division by
zero in the backward node; in that pathological case the gradient is
not statistically meaningful but is well-defined.

members.name: view_op
members.signature: int view_op(const int & a, const int & new_shape)
members.summary: Reshape that never copies: the result always shares `a`'s storage.
members.extended:
The same view `reshape_op` makes when `a`'s elements read in place
as `new_shape` — a dense tensor on either device, or a strided view whose
new shape only drops or inserts size-1 axes.  Where reshape_op would copy
instead (`x.t().view(-1)`), this raises.

raises.description: The element counts differ, or `-1` cannot be inferred.
`a` cannot be viewed as `new_shape` without a copy.

members.name: vstack_op
members.summary: Vertically stack a sequence of tensors.
members.extended:
Equivalent to NumPy `vstack`: 1-D inputs of length `N` are promoted to
row vectors and stacked into a 2-D tensor of shape `(len(xs), N)`;
inputs with rank >= 2 are concatenated along axis 0.

**See Also**

`hstack_op`, `stack_op`.

parameters.name: xs
parameters.description: Non-empty list of tensors.  For rank >= 2, every dim except axis 0 must agree; for 1-D inputs, lengths must agree.

returns.description: Vertically stacked tensor with rank `max(2, input_rank)`.

members.name: where_op
members.signature: int where_op(const int & cond, const int & x, const int & y)
members.summary: Element-wise conditional selection between two tensors.
members.extended:
Returns `x` at positions where `cond` is true, otherwise `y`.
This is the tensor analogue of the ternary expression
`cond ? x : y` applied element-wise.

**Math**

$$\mathrm{out}_i = \begin{cases} x_i & \text{if } \mathrm{cond}_i \\
y_i & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

**Shape**

On the GPU stream all three operands are broadcast by the MLX backend.
On the CPU stream all three must share the same shape.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Values selected at positions where `cond` is true.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Values selected at positions where `cond` is false.

returns.description: Tensor of the broadcast shape and dtype of `x`/`y`.

notes:
Backward propagates `grad_out` masked by `cond` to `x` and masked
by `~cond` to `y`.  `cond` itself receives no gradient.

members.name: wrap_dim
members.signature: int wrap_dim(int dim, int ndim, const char * op)
members.summary: Resolve one signed `dim` against a tensor of rank `ndim`.
members.extended:
The rule every dim argument follows.  A 0-d tensor answers to `dim` 0
and -1 as if it had one axis, as the reference does; the result is then 0
and names no real axis, so an op that indexes `shape()[dim]` must take
the 0-d case apart first (`ops/utils/ScalarAxis.h`).

raises.description: `dim` falls outside `[-max(ndim, 1), max(ndim, 1))`.

members.name: zero_derivative_through
members.signature: int zero_derivative_through(int grad, const int & source)
members.summary: `grad` kept in the graph through `source` with derivative zero.
members.extended:
For a graph-mode formula that reads `source` only through a comparison
— relu masks the incoming gradient by `x <= 0`.  The reference's
backward of such an op is itself an op of `x` (`threshold_backward`),
so the gradient it returns requires grad and a second derivative through
it is zeros; a comparison carries no graph, so without this the result
came back detached and a second derivative raised.  A gradient no
formula built from `source` — that of a linear function — is a
constant and stays detached, as the reference has it.

Returns `grad` itself when it already requires grad, when `source`
does not, or outside graph mode.
